To explain how Latin translators changed the meaning of the word "algebra"
To describe the rules of inheritance that were followed in ninth-century Baghdad
questions.e: The text notes the book's legacy in the words 'algebra' and 'algorithm', then stresses with 'Yet' its practical problems. Inheritance appears only as one example of those problems, and no claim is made that he invented all of modern mathematics.

questions.s:
A study in a Lahore school found that students who took a short walk before a maths test scored slightly higher than those who sat quietly beforehand. The walkers also said they felt less nervous. The researchers caution that the study was small and lasted only a month. Still, they say, a ten-minute walk costs nothing and may be worth trying before exams.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To compare the maths results of schools in Lahore with those of other cities
To argue that schools should replace some classroom lessons with outdoor exercise
To report a small study's finding and a possible use, along with a caution
To explain how walking improves the flow of blood to the brain during tests
questions.e: The text gives the result, the researchers' warning about the study's size, and their modest suggestion to try a walk. It offers no biological explanation and no proposal to cut lessons.

questions.s:
The poem opens in a crowded bazaar: shouting vendors, a donkey cart, the smell of frying pakoras. Gradually the noise fades as the speaker walks home through narrowing lanes. By the final stanza, she is alone on a rooftop, and the only sound is a kite string humming in the wind. The movement from crowd to solitude mirrors the speaker's own shift from distraction to quiet reflection.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It compares two poems about bazaars and explains why one is more vivid than the other one.
It describes a poem's setting and then argues that the poem's ending is weaker than its opening.
It summarises the events of a poem and then describes the life of the poet who wrote it.
It traces a poem's shift from one setting to another and then interprets that shift.
questions.e: The first three sentences follow the poem from bazaar to rooftop, and the last explains that this movement mirrors the speaker's inner change. Only one poem is discussed, and the ending is interpreted, not judged weaker.

questions.s:
People often describe the placebo effect as "all in the mind," as if it were imaginary. Yet the effect can be measured. In some studies of pain, patients given sugar pills reported less pain, and brain scans showed reduced activity in regions linked to pain. This does not mean placebos can cure disease; their effects are strongest for symptoms such as pain and nausea, and weakest for conditions such as infections.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It cites a common description, offers evidence that confirms it, and recommends that doctors use placebos.
It cites a common description, offers evidence that complicates it, and argues that placebos cure most diseases.
It cites a common description, offers evidence that complicates it, and then sets limits on the effect.
It describes a single experiment, criticises the way it was designed, and calls for more careful research.
questions.e: The text quotes 'all in the mind', presents measurable pain effects that complicate it, and then says placebos do not cure disease. The option claiming placebos cure most diseases begins correctly but contradicts the final sentence's limits.

questions.s:
Most of the tea drunk in Pakistan is imported, much of it from Kenya. Since the 1980s, researchers have tested whether tea could be grown in the hills around Shinkiari in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the climate and acidic soils seemed suitable. The trial plots produced good-quality leaves. Large-scale planting, however, has been slow, partly because tea bushes take several years to become productive and farmers can earn money faster from other crops.

Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence in the text?
o: It offers reasons why a promising trial has not led to widespread planting.
It describes the methods researchers used to test the quality of the leaves.
It argues that farmers should give up their other crops and plant tea instead.
It explains why the hills around Shinkiari have acidic soils that suit tea.
questions.e: After the good trial results, 'however' introduces slow uptake and its causes: years before bushes produce and quicker profits elsewhere. The sentence explains farmers' choices without telling them to change.

questions.s:
When the power failed in the middle of the cricket final, the whole street groaned. Within minutes, though, someone had found a battery radio, and the neighbours gathered around it on plastic chairs. For the next two hours, they listened to the commentary together, cheering each boundary as loudly as if they could see it. Several later said it was the best match they had ever watched, or rather, heard.

Which choice best describes the function of the sentence "Within minutes, though, someone had found a battery radio, and the neighbours gathered around it on plastic chairs." in the text?
o: It describes how the cricket final was finally won by the home team.
It explains why the power failed in the middle of the cricket final.
It reveals that the neighbours preferred listening on the radio to watching television.
It shows how the neighbours responded to the disappointment of the power cut.
questions.e: After the groan at the power cut, 'though' introduces the neighbours' quick solution of gathering round a radio. Their later enjoyment does not mean they preferred radio in general, and the cause of the power cut and the result of the match are never given.

questions.s:
Paper money depends on trust. A banknote has almost no value as paper; it is useful only because people believe others will accept it in exchange for goods. When that belief weakens, as during periods of very high inflation, people may rush to swap their notes for gold, foreign currency or anything else likely to hold its value. A currency's strength, then, rests as much on confidence as on the economy behind it.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To compare the strength of several currencies during periods of high inflation
To explain that the value of paper money depends largely on confidence
To argue that people should keep their savings in gold rather than in banknotes
To describe the process by which banknotes are designed and then printed
questions.e: The text opens with 'Paper money depends on trust' and ends by tying a currency's strength to confidence. Swapping notes for gold is described as what people do when trust fails, not recommended.

questions.s:
Critics have often called the novel's ending abrupt: the heroine, after three hundred pages of indecision, accepts the job abroad in a single sentence. But the abruptness may be the point. Throughout the book, decisions are delayed by family meetings, letters and second opinions. By letting the final decision happen almost without discussion, the novelist shows the heroine at last acting for herself.

Which choice best describes the function of the sentence "But the abruptness may be the point." in the text?
o: It introduces a summary of the events that lead to the heroine's decision.
It agrees with the critics that the novel's ending was written too hastily.
It suggests that the heroine's decision to go abroad was a serious mistake.
It recasts a feature that critics saw as a flaw as a deliberate choice.
questions.e: The critics call the ending abrupt, and 'But' introduces the view that the abruptness is intentional, which the rest of the text explains. The sentence disputes rather than accepts the critics' complaint.

questions.s:
Honeybees share the location of food through a "waggle dance." A returning forager moves in a figure-of-eight pattern on the honeycomb, waggling her body during the straight central run. The angle of that run relative to vertical shows the direction of the food relative to the Sun, and the length of the waggle indicates the distance. Other bees follow the dancer and then fly out to find the food themselves.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It names a behaviour, describes how it is done, explains what its parts signal, and gives its result.
It names a behaviour, describes it briefly, and argues that it is less precise than was once believed.
It compares the behaviour of honeybees with that of other insects that also find food by dancing.
It names a behaviour, explains how scientists first discovered it, and describes the debate it caused.
questions.e: The text names the waggle dance, describes the figure-of-eight, explains that angle and length signal direction and distance, and ends with other bees finding the food. It says nothing about discovery, debate or precision.

questions.s:
The Deosai Plains in Gilgit-Baltistan lie more than 4,000 metres above sea level and are covered by snow for much of the year. In summer, however, they bloom with wildflowers and become home to marmots, foxes and one of the last populations of Himalayan brown bears in the region. A national park was created there partly to protect the bears, whose numbers have slowly increased since then.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To compare the Himalayan brown bear with other kinds of bear
To describe a high-altitude area and the wildlife it protects
To argue that more tourists should visit Gilgit-Baltistan in summer
To explain why snow covers the Deosai Plains for most of the year
questions.e: The text describes the plains' height and seasons, their summer wildlife, and the park that protects the bears. The snow is mentioned but not explained, and tourism is never discussed.

questions.s:
The researcher had expected that students who highlighted their textbooks would remember more than those who simply read them. Her results showed no difference. Puzzled, she interviewed the students and found that many highlighters had marked nearly every line, so the highlighting no longer singled anything out. She now advises students to highlight no more than one sentence per paragraph.

Which choice best describes the function of the sentence "Puzzled, she interviewed the students and found that many highlighters had marked nearly every line, so the highlighting no longer singled anything out." in the text?
o: It shows that the researcher doubted the accuracy of her original results.
It explains why the students preferred highlighting to simply reading.
It describes how the researcher found a likely reason for an unexpected result.
It presents the advice the researcher now gives to students who highlight.
questions.e: The 'no difference' result surprised her, and the interviews revealed why: marking nearly everything highlights nothing. She sought an explanation rather than doubting the data, and the advice comes in the next sentence.

questions.s:
In many Pakistani cities, informal waste pickers collect plastic bottles, paper and metal from streets and dumps and sell them to recycling dealers. Their work is rarely counted in official figures, yet studies suggest they recover a large share of the recyclable material that would otherwise be buried or burned. Some city governments have begun offering them identity cards and protective gloves in recognition of this role.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To explain how recycling dealers turn plastic bottles into new products
To argue that city governments should take over all recycling from waste pickers
To describe the health risks that waste pickers face while working on dumps
To highlight the overlooked contribution of informal waste pickers
questions.e: The text says the pickers' work is 'rarely counted' yet recovers much recyclable material, and notes official recognition. It never proposes replacing them, and health risks are only hinted at by the gloves.

questions.s:
For centuries, doctors applied leeches to patients in the mistaken belief that removing blood cured many illnesses. By the late nineteenth century, the practice had largely been abandoned as useless. Surprisingly, leeches have returned to some hospitals. After surgery to reattach a finger or an ear, blood can collect in the tissue, and leeches remove it while releasing a substance that keeps it flowing.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It describes a discredited practice, its decline, and its return in a new, narrower role.
It compares two kinds of surgery and explains why one needs leeches while the other does not.
It describes a practice, its decline, and the reasons doctors still refuse to use it today.
It describes a practice, explains why it was always effective, and urges its wider use today.
questions.e: The text moves from old bloodletting with leeches, to its abandonment, to their limited modern use after reattachment surgery. The text calls the old belief 'mistaken', so the practice was not always effective, and doctors now do use leeches.

questions.s:
Saad had never liked mornings. His alarm rang at six every day, and he usually pressed snooze three times before he dragged himself out of bed. But on the first day of his summer job at the zoo, he was dressed and waiting at the gate before the keepers arrived. The chance to help feed the giraffes, it seemed, was stronger than any alarm clock.

Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text?
o: It suggests that Saad arrived late on his first day at work.
It explains why Saad dislikes waking up early in the morning.
It shows a change in Saad's usual behaviour.
It describes the duties of the keepers who feed the giraffes.
questions.e: After two sentences about Saad's dislike of mornings, 'But' shows him arriving before the keepers, a clear change. He arrives early, not late, and the keepers' duties are not described.

questions.s:
The phrase "survival of the fittest" is often taken to mean that the strongest or most aggressive animals win out in nature. Biologists use "fitness" differently: it refers to how successfully an organism survives and reproduces in its particular environment. A small, shy bird that hides well and raises many chicks may be far fitter than a large, bold one that is often caught by predators.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To explain how predators choose which of the birds they will hunt
To clarify what a familiar scientific term actually means
To argue that small birds are generally more successful than large ones
To describe how the phrase "survival of the fittest" first came into use
questions.e: The text contrasts the popular reading of 'fittest' with biologists' meaning and illustrates it with two birds. The birds are an example of the definition, not a general claim that small birds do better.

questions.s:
For years, the textile mill measured success by a single number: metres of cloth produced per day. Managers rewarded the shifts that produced the most. Gradually, however, complaints from buyers increased, because workers rushing to raise their numbers were letting faulty cloth pass. The mill now records both output and the share of cloth that buyers return because of defects.

Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text?
o: It explains how the managers decided which of the shifts deserved rewards.
It identifies an unintended effect of the way the mill measured success.
It argues that the workers were careless because they were poorly trained.
It describes the new method that the mill now uses to record its results.
questions.e: Rewarding output alone led workers to rush and pass faulty cloth, an effect nobody intended, and the last sentence shows the fix. The text blames the incentive, not poor training.

questions.s:
Scholars debate whether the Silk Road should be called a "road" at all. There was no single route: goods moved along a shifting web of paths across deserts, mountains and seas, and few traders travelled the whole distance from China to the Mediterranean. Most carried goods for a short stretch before selling them to others. The name, invented by a nineteenth-century geographer, may therefore suggest more unity than ever existed.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It describes a trade route, lists the goods carried along it, and explains why trade along it finally ended.
It raises a question about a name, presents evidence in its favour, and concludes that the name is accurate.
It describes the life of a geographer and explains why he decided to invent a famous name.
It raises a question about a name, presents relevant evidence, and concludes that the name may mislead.
questions.e: The text asks whether 'road' fits, shows there was no single route or through-traveller, and concludes ('therefore') that the name suggests false unity. The evidence counts against the name, so the option calling the name accurate reverses the conclusion.

questions.s:
Many students believe that rereading their notes is the best way to prepare for an exam. Research suggests otherwise. Students who test themselves, by answering practice questions or explaining ideas aloud without looking at their notes, tend to remember far more a week later than students who spend the same time rereading. Self-testing feels harder, which may be why it is less popular, but that effort seems to be what strengthens memory.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To challenge a common study habit and recommend a more effective one
To explain why exams are a poor way of measuring what students know
To argue that students should stop taking notes during their lessons
To describe how teachers write practice questions for their own classes
questions.e: The text questions rereading ('Research suggests otherwise') and presents self-testing as better for memory. Notes are still used in self-testing; the point is how to study them.

questions.s:
When an Italian expedition made the first ascent of K2 in 1954, newspapers celebrated the two climbers who reached the summit. Far less attention went to Amir Mahdi, a high-altitude porter from Hunza, who helped carry oxygen bottles toward the top camp and was forced to spend a night in the open above 8,000 metres, losing his toes to frostbite. Historians of mountaineering now point to his story as an example of how the roles of local porters were often overlooked.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To argue that the Italian climbers did not really reach the summit of K2
To describe the dangers that all climbers face above 8,000 metres
To draw attention to a porter's overlooked role in a famous climb
To explain why the first ascent of K2 needed bottled oxygen to succeed
questions.e: The text contrasts the praise for the summit climbers with the neglect of Amir Mahdi's dangerous work. It accepts that the summit was reached, and the night in the open is part of his story, not a general account of dangers.

questions.s:
Some clothing companies have promised to use only recycled polyester, made from plastic bottles. This sounds like a clear environmental gain. But critics note that once bottles become clothing, they are rarely recycled again, whereas bottles can often be recycled several times as bottles. Washing polyester clothes also releases tiny plastic fibres into rivers and seas. The promise, critics say, may move the problem rather than solve it.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It compares two kinds of fabric and explains why one of them is more comfortable to wear.
It describes the way plastic bottles are turned into fabric, step by step, in a modern factory.
It describes a promise, notes its apparent benefit, and presents objections that question that benefit.
It describes a promise, praises its benefits, and urges other companies to make the same commitment.
questions.e: The text states the promise, grants that it 'sounds like' a gain, and then gives critics' objections about recycling and fibres. The benefit is questioned, not praised, and the manufacturing steps are not described.

questions.s:
In the centre of the village stands a banyan tree said to be more than two hundred years old. Its branches send down roots that grow into new trunks, so the tree now covers an area larger than a football pitch. Under its shade, elders settle disputes, children do homework and traders sell vegetables on market days. For the villagers, the tree is less a plant than a meeting place.

Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text?
o: It explains how the banyan's hanging roots grow down into new trunks.
It describes the vegetables that traders sell on market days.
It suggests that the elders own the land on which the tree stands.
It gives examples of how villagers use the space beneath the tree.
questions.e: The third sentence lists activities under the tree, which supports the final point that it is a meeting place. The roots are explained in the second sentence, and vegetables are mentioned only as one activity.

questions.s:
Film music is designed, in a sense, not to be noticed. A good score guides an audience's feelings, building tension before a chase or softening a sad farewell, without drawing attention to itself. Viewers asked about a film's music afterwards often cannot hum a single theme, even though the same scenes played in silence leave them noticeably less moved. The music works, in other words, precisely because they do not notice it.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To describe how film music affects audiences without their full awareness
To argue that most film music is forgettable because it is poorly composed
To explain how composers write the music that accompanies chase scenes
To compare the effects of silent films with those of films that use music
questions.e: The text says a good score shapes feelings without being noticed, shown by viewers who forget the music yet are less moved without it. Forgetting the tune is presented as a sign of skill, not poor composition.

questions.s:
A survey found that people who own dogs walk more than people who do not. It would be tempting to conclude that getting a dog makes people more active. But the survey cannot show this. People who already enjoy walking may simply be more likely to choose a dog as a pet. To test whether dogs cause more walking, researchers would need to track people's activity before and after they got one.

Which choice best describes the function of the sentence "But the survey cannot show this." in the text?
o: It introduces evidence showing that dogs make their owners less active.
It warns that a conclusion drawn from the survey goes beyond its evidence.
It explains why people who enjoy walking prefer dogs to other pets.
It suggests that the survey's finding about dog owners' walking was inaccurate.
questions.e: The sentence rejects the causal conclusion, and the next sentences explain why: active people may choose dogs. It accepts the survey's finding that owners walk more; what it doubts is the leap from correlation to cause.

questions.s:
Ajrak, the block-printed cloth of Sindh, is famous for its deep blue and red patterns. Making it is slow work. The cloth is washed and softened, then printed with carved wooden blocks using a paste that resists dye. It is dyed, washed, printed again and dyed again, through many rounds that can take two weeks or more. Each stage adds a layer of colour, which is why a true ajrak can look so rich.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It introduces a product, explains its history, and argues that machine-made versions are equally good.
It introduces a product, describes how it is made, and links that process to its quality.
It compares two kinds of cloth and explains why one of them is more expensive to make.
It describes a product, lists the places where it is sold, and explains how its price is set.
questions.e: The text introduces ajrak, describes washing, block printing and repeated dyeing, and ends by tying the layers to its rich colour. No history, comparison or price is given.

questions.s:
Earthquakes cannot yet be predicted, but the damage they cause can be reduced. In Japan, strict building codes require structures that sway rather than crack, and schoolchildren practise drills several times a year. After the 2005 earthquake in northern Pakistan, engineers and planners studied such measures to see which could be adapted to local villages, where many homes are built of stone without reinforcement.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To explain why earthquakes happen more often in Japan than in Pakistan
To argue that scientists will soon be able to predict earthquakes precisely
To show that the harm caused by earthquakes can be reduced through planning
To describe the damage that the 2005 earthquake caused to northern villages
questions.e: The first sentence states the main idea, and the Japanese and Pakistani examples show planning reducing harm. The text says earthquakes cannot yet be predicted and does not compare how often they occur.

questions.s:
For centuries, sailors feared scurvy, a disease that caused bleeding gums and exhaustion on long voyages. In 1747, a ship's surgeon named James Lind gave different remedies to groups of sick sailors and found that those given oranges and lemons recovered fastest. Strangely, his finding was not fully put into practice for decades, partly because Lind himself did not believe that citrus fruit was the only cure.

Which choice best describes the function of the sentence "Strangely, his finding was not fully put into practice for decades, partly because Lind himself did not believe that citrus fruit was the only cure." in the text?
o: It explains how Lind divided the sick sailors into separate groups.
It describes the symptoms that scurvy caused on long sea voyages.
It argues that Lind's experiment was poorly designed and unreliable.
It notes a surprising delay in acting on a discovery and suggests one cause.
questions.e: 'Strangely' marks the delay as surprising, and 'partly because' gives Lind's own doubts as a reason. The sentence questions what Lind concluded, not how well the experiment was designed.

questions.s:
For many people, the word "desert" suggests sand dunes stretching to the horizon. Yet most of the world's deserts are not sandy at all. Deserts are defined by low rainfall, not by sand, and many are covered by gravel, bare rock or even ice. By that definition, Antarctica, the coldest and windiest continent, is also the largest desert on Earth.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To correct a common idea of what makes a place a desert
To compare the temperatures of hot deserts with those of cold ones
To explain how sand dunes form and then move across deserts
To argue that Antarctica should no longer be called a continent
questions.e: The text replaces the sand-dune image with the real definition, low rainfall, and uses Antarctica as a striking example. Antarctica is called a continent and a desert; nothing suggests renaming it.

questions.s:
Astronomers have long complained that city lights hide the stars. Ecologists add another concern: many animals use darkness as a cue. Migrating birds can be drawn off course by brightly lit buildings, and newly hatched sea turtles may crawl toward street lamps instead of the sea. Neither group, however, is calling for cities to go dark. Their proposals are modest: shielding lamps so that light falls downward, and dimming lights when streets are empty.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To argue that cities should switch off all their streetlights to protect wildlife
To explain how migrating birds use the stars and the moon to find their way
To present concerns about night lighting and the modest changes proposed in response
To show that astronomers and ecologists disagree about how cities should be lit
questions.e: The text gives astronomers' and ecologists' concerns, then stresses that their proposals are limited to shielding and dimming. 'Neither group... is calling for cities to go dark' rules out switching off all lights, and the two groups agree rather than disagree.

questions.s:
Zara's science project began with a question: does salt water freeze faster than fresh water? She filled two identical cups, one with tap water and one with salty water, and placed them side by side in the freezer. She checked them every fifteen minutes. The tap water froze first, and the salty water took much longer, which Zara later learned is because salt lowers the freezing point of water.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It poses a question, explains why it cannot be tested, and suggests a different question.
It poses a question, describes a test of it, and reports the result with an explanation.
It compares two freezers and explains why one of them works better than the other.
It describes a result and then explains why Zara's teacher disagreed with the result.
questions.e: The text asks the question, describes the two-cup test, and gives the result along with the reason (salt lowers the freezing point). The question is tested, not abandoned, and only one freezer is used.

questions.s:
Every few years, a newspaper announces the "death" of the printed book. E-readers, phones and audiobooks are expected to make paper obsolete. Yet sales figures tell a different story. In many countries, printed books still outsell e-books by a wide margin, and some young readers say they prefer paper because it lets them escape, for a while, from their screens.

Which choice best describes the function of the sentence "Yet sales figures tell a different story." in the text?
o: It introduces evidence that confirms the newspapers' predictions about books.
It explains why e-readers have become more popular among young readers.
It questions whether sales figures can show how much people actually read.
It signals that evidence will contradict the prediction described before it.
questions.e: 'Yet' and 'a different story' turn from the predicted death of print to figures showing print still outselling e-books. The evidence works against the prediction, and the young readers mentioned prefer paper, not e-readers.

questions.s:
Early maps of the world often placed the mapmaker's own country at the centre. It is easy to see this as simple vanity. A more generous reading is that mapmakers drew what they knew best in the greatest detail and placed it where viewers' eyes fall first. Distant lands, described only in travellers' reports, were pushed to the edges, where errors mattered less. The central position, in other words, may reflect knowledge as much as pride.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It describes a feature of old maps, mentions one explanation, and proposes a more generous alternative.
It compares maps from two countries and argues that one of them was drawn with greater accuracy.
It describes a feature of old maps and concludes that mapmakers were moved by pride alone.
It describes a feature of old maps, offers one explanation, and then presents evidence proving that explanation.
questions.e: The text notes the centred home country, mentions vanity, and offers the knowledge-based reading as an alternative. The final sentence says 'knowledge as much as pride', so 'pride alone' contradicts it, and vanity is never proved.

questions.s:
Wasim's cousin from Toronto arrived in Lahore a week before the family wedding. At first she spoke Urdu slowly and kept checking words on her phone. By the third day, though, she was bargaining in the cloth market and joking with the aunties as if she had never left. Wasim realised that she had understood far more than she had let on.

Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text?
o: It describes the cloth that the cousin bought at the market.
It reveals that Wasim had taught his cousin how to speak Urdu.
It shows a change in the cousin's confidence in a new setting.
It explains why the cousin had travelled to Lahore for the wedding.
questions.e: The cousin's hesitant Urdu in the second sentence gives way, with 'though', to confident bargaining and joking. No purchases or lessons from Wasim are described.

questions.s:
Volcanic eruptions can cool the planet. When Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted in 1991, it threw millions of tonnes of sulphur gas into the upper atmosphere, where it formed tiny droplets that reflected sunlight. Average global temperatures fell by about half a degree Celsius over the following year. Some scientists have studied this effect as a possible, though controversial, way of slowing global warming.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To explain how an eruption cooled the Earth and why scientists study the effect
To describe the damage that the 1991 eruption caused in the Philippines
To argue that volcanic eruptions are the main cause of climate change today
To warn that releasing sulphur gas into the air would end global warming
questions.e: The text explains the sulphur droplets that cooled the planet after Pinatubo and mentions research into the effect. It calls the idea 'controversial', not a sure way to end warming, and gives no account of local damage.

questions.s:
The jury of the design competition had expected entries for the new bus shelter to focus on appearance. Most did. One entry, from a pair of engineering students, instead began with a survey of passengers, who said their main complaints were heat and a lack of information about arrival times. The students' simple shelter, with a shaded roof and a solar-powered timetable screen, won first prize.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
o: It describes a competition, lists the rules for entries, and explains how the jury scored each design.
It states an expectation, notes that most entries met it, and describes one that took another approach.
It describes a survey of passengers and explains why most of them prefer to travel by car.
It compares the appearance of several bus shelters and argues that the most attractive should win.
questions.e: The text gives the jury's expectation, confirms most entries matched it ('Most did'), then describes the students' survey-based design that won. The winning shelter was chosen for function, not looks, and no rules or scoring are given.

questions.s:
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould growing on one of his plates of bacteria had killed the bacteria around it. The story is often told as a lucky accident. But luck alone does not explain it. Others had probably seen similar moulds and thrown their plates away; Fleming recognised that the clear ring around the mould was worth investigating. As Louis Pasteur once said, chance favours the prepared mind.

Which choice best describes the function of the sentence "But luck alone does not explain it." in the text?
o: It denies that Fleming's discovery involved any element of chance at all.
It introduces the claim that other scientists discovered penicillin first.
It explains why the mould killed the bacteria growing around it.
It challenges a common account by suggesting that another factor also mattered.
questions.e: The word 'alone' keeps luck in the story while adding Fleming's readiness to notice the mould, which the next sentence describes. Denying any chance overstates the point, and the others 'had probably seen' moulds without discovering anything.

questions.s:
Economists often measure a country's well-being by its gross domestic product (GDP), the total value of the goods and services it produces. Critics point out that GDP rises when a country spends money cleaning up after a flood or treating victims of air pollution, even though no one is better off. It also ignores unpaid work, such as caring for children or elderly relatives. These critics do not propose discarding GDP, but they argue that it should be read alongside other measures.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
o: To explain why some critics think a common economic measure is incomplete
To show that floods and pollution make a country's economy grow stronger
To explain how governments calculate the value of unpaid work at home
To argue that GDP should be abandoned in favour of measures of happiness
questions.e: The text gives critics' two points, that GDP counts harmful spending and ignores unpaid work, and their aim of supplementing it. The last sentence says they 'do not propose discarding GDP', which rules out abandoning it.

questions.s:
Text 1
Many teachers assign homework every evening, believing that regular practice at home is the surest way for students to master new material. A daily assignment, they argue, builds discipline and helps students notice what they have not yet understood before the next lesson. Without it, they warn, lessons fade quickly from memory and students fall behind.

Text 2
A review of studies on homework found little link between the amount of homework assigned in primary schools and pupils' test results. For older students the link was stronger, but only up to about two hours a night; beyond that, results did not improve. The researchers suggest that for young children, time spent reading for pleasure or playing outdoors may be just as valuable as written assignments.

Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the teachers' view in Text 1?
o: They would claim that older students should be given more than two hours of homework a night.
They would agree that students of every age benefit from homework that is assigned each evening.
They would say daily homework may help older students but does little for young children.
They would argue that homework lowers the test results of students in every age group.
questions.e: The review found a link only for older students, and none beyond two hours, while young children gained little. It finds no benefit past two hours, not harm, so it neither supports homework for all ages nor claims homework lowers results.

questions.s:
Text 1
When astronomers voted in 2006 to reclassify Pluto as a "dwarf planet," many people protested. For them, Pluto had been the ninth planet since its discovery in 1930, and removing it seemed an arbitrary decision by a small committee. Some argued that tradition and public affection should count for something in deciding what a planet is.

Text 2
The reclassification of Pluto followed a simple scientific logic. Astronomers had discovered several objects in the outer solar system similar in size to Pluto, including one, Eris, that is slightly more massive. Either all of them had to be called planets, or a clear definition was needed. A planet, the astronomers decided, must have cleared its orbit of other large bodies, which Pluto has not done.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the protesters described in Text 1?
o: By arguing that Eris should also have been removed from the official list of planets
By agreeing that public affection should help decide which objects are called planets
By pointing out that Pluto is larger than every other object in the outer solar system
By explaining that the decision followed a consistent rule, not an arbitrary one
questions.e: Text 2 presents the change as the result of a clear rule needed once similar objects were found, answering the charge of arbitrariness. It says Eris is more massive than Pluto, and it gives no weight to tradition or affection.

questions.s:
Text 1
Studies comparing reading on paper with reading on screens have often found that people remember less of what they read on a screen, especially long, complex texts. One explanation is that screens encourage skimming: readers used to scrolling quickly through messages bring the same hurried habits to serious reading, even when a text demands close attention.

Text 2
The so-called screen penalty may not be fixed. In a recent study, students who were told to read carefully and were given more time performed just as well on screens as on paper. The difference, the researchers concluded, lies less in the screen itself than in the reading habits people bring to it, and habits can be changed.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
o: It accepts the habit-based explanation in Text 1 but suggests that the effect can be overcome.
It argues that reading on paper encourages skimming even more than reading on screens does.
It offers new evidence that screens themselves damage readers' memory for complex texts.
It rejects the finding in Text 1 that people tend to remember less of what they read on screens.
questions.e: Text 2 agrees that habits, not screens, cause the gap, and adds that changed instructions removed it. It does not deny the usual finding; it calls the penalty 'not fixed', which assumes the penalty normally exists.

questions.s:
Text 1
Modern zoos argue that they play an important role in conservation. By breeding endangered species in captivity, they keep alive populations that might otherwise disappear, and some animals bred in zoos, such as the Arabian oryx, have been successfully returned to the wild. Zoos also teach millions of visitors each year about the threats facing wildlife.

Text 2
Critics of zoos accept that a few breeding programmes have saved species from extinction. But they point out that most animals in zoos are not endangered at all, and only a small number of species have ever been released back into the wild. For the majority of animals kept in zoos, they argue, conservation is a justification rather than the true purpose.

Based on the texts, how would the critics in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 about conservation?
o: By arguing that no species has ever been saved from extinction by a zoo's breeding programme
By granting some successes while denying that conservation explains most of what zoos do
By agreeing that conservation is the main reason that most animals are kept in zoos today
By claiming that teaching visitors about wildlife matters more than breeding endangered species
questions.e: The critics 'accept that a few breeding programmes have saved species' but say most zoo animals are not endangered, so conservation is mostly a justification. Saying no species was ever saved contradicts that concession.

questions.s:
Text 1
Several schools in Islamabad have proposed starting classes an hour later, at nine o'clock. Studies show that teenagers' body clocks shift during adolescence, making it hard for them to fall asleep early. Supporters believe that a later start would leave students more alert in lessons and, over time, improve their marks.

Text 2
Parents' groups have opposed the plan to start school later. Many parents leave for work at eight, and a later start would leave younger children unsupervised in the morning or force families to arrange extra transport. Whatever the benefits for sleep, they argue, a school timetable must also work for the families who depend on it.

Which choice best describes a difference in focus between the two texts?
o: Text 1 focuses on younger children, while Text 2 focuses on adults who work during the night.
Text 1 focuses on students' sleep, while Text 2 focuses on the practical needs of families.
Text 1 focuses on teachers' working hours, while Text 2 focuses on teenagers' changing body clocks.
Text 1 focuses on transport costs, while Text 2 focuses on the marks students get in examinations.
questions.e: Text 1 supports the later start because of teenagers' body clocks and alertness, while Text 2 raises work schedules, supervision and transport. Transport appears only in Text 2, and body clocks only in Text 1.

questions.s:
Text 1
The symbols found on Indus Valley seals have resisted every attempt at decipherment. Most scholars assume that they record a written language, perhaps an early form of a language family still spoken in South Asia. The main obstacle is the shortness of the inscriptions: most contain only about five signs, and no text giving the same words in a known language has been found.

Text 2
A few researchers have questioned whether the Indus signs are writing at all. They note that the inscriptions are extremely short and that many signs appear only once in the entire known collection. Such signs, they suggest, might be symbols of clans, offices or gods, closer to emblems than to words.

Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption described in Text 1?
o: They would doubt it, citing the same feature that Text 1 treats as an obstacle to decipherment.
They would reject it, arguing that a bilingual text has shown the signs to be emblems.
They would support it, but argue that the language belonged to a different language family.
They would accept it, since very short inscriptions are typical of early written languages.
questions.e: Text 1 sees short inscriptions as a barrier to reading the script, while Text 2 uses that same shortness to question whether it is writing at all. Text 1 says no bilingual text has been found, and Text 2 never claims one.

questions.s:
Text 1
Since 2020, many software companies in Lahore and Karachi have allowed their staff to work from home. Managers report that productivity has stayed the same or even risen, and employees save hours each week that they once spent commuting through heavy traffic. Several firms have given up part of their office space altogether.

Text 2
Working from home has costs that productivity figures do not show. Junior employees, in particular, say they learn less when they cannot watch experienced colleagues solve problems or ask quick questions at the next desk. Some companies have therefore begun asking new staff to spend at least three days a week in the office.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the managers' reports in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that working from home has no real disadvantages for any of the employees
By claiming that the time spent commuting in Lahore and Karachi has actually decreased
By suggesting that the reports may overlook a cost to less experienced workers
By arguing that productivity has in fact fallen sharply at most of these companies
questions.e: Text 2 says productivity figures miss a hidden cost: junior staff learn less at home. It does not dispute the figures themselves, only what they leave out.

questions.s:
Text 1
At the end of the novel, Sameena leaves her village for the city, and most readers see the ending as a triumph. She has escaped the narrow expectations of her family and is free, at last, to pursue her studies. Her final words, a cheerful promise to write home every week, seem to confirm the note of hope.

Text 2
The ending is less triumphant than it first appears. In the final chapter, Sameena looks back at the village from the bus window and feels "something tear." The novelist gives her freedom, but she also makes clear what that freedom costs: the only home Sameena has ever known. Even the cheerful promise to write home reads, on a second look, like an attempt to hold on.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of the ending in Text 1?
o: By claiming that Sameena's family supported her decision to move to the city
By arguing that Sameena does not actually leave her village at the end of the novel
By agreeing that the ending is a simple triumph with no sense of sadness in it
By accepting that Sameena gains freedom but stressing what she loses
questions.e: Text 2 says 'The novelist gives her freedom' but points to the tearing feeling as a sign of what she loses. It calls the ending 'less triumphant', not untriumphant, so it qualifies rather than reverses Text 1's reading.

questions.s:
Text 1
Raising the minimum wage, some economists warn, can backfire. If employers must pay more for each worker, they may hire fewer people, cut working hours or replace workers with machines. The very workers the policy aims to help could then find themselves without jobs, or with less income than before the rise.

Text 2
Studies of actual minimum wage increases have often found much smaller job losses than simple models predict, and sometimes none at all. One reason may be that better-paid workers are less likely to quit, which saves employers the cost of constantly hiring and training replacements. Higher pay may also increase spending in local shops, creating demand that supports jobs.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the warning in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that higher minimum wages usually lead employers to replace workers with machines
By claiming that employers would rather hire and train new workers than keep their old ones
By noting that evidence from real wage rises often shows less harm than the warning predicts
By arguing that minimum wage increases always create a large number of new jobs for workers
questions.e: Text 2 reports 'much smaller job losses than simple models predict' and suggests lower staff turnover as a reason. It does not say rises always create jobs; at best it found no losses in some cases.

questions.s:
Text 1
For most of the twentieth century, dinosaurs were pictured as scaly, slow-moving reptiles, more like giant lizards than any living animal. Museum models and films showed them dragging heavy tails along the ground. Their extinction was often treated as proof that they were evolutionary failures, too slow and clumsy to survive.

Text 2
Fossils discovered since the 1990s, many of them in China, have transformed our picture of dinosaurs. Some show clear traces of feathers, and studies of bones suggest that many dinosaurs were active and grew quickly. Most palaeontologists now regard birds as the living descendants of one group of dinosaurs, so in a sense dinosaurs never fully disappeared.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
o: It explains why dinosaurs died out, a question that Text 1 leaves completely unanswered.
It argues that the films mentioned in Text 1 were more accurate than the museum models.
It offers new fossil evidence that supports the picture of dinosaurs described in Text 1.
It presents discoveries that have replaced the older picture of dinosaurs given in Text 1.
questions.e: Text 1 describes the old image of slow, scaly reptiles, and Text 2 reports feathered, active dinosaurs that 'transformed our picture'. The new fossils contradict rather than support the older image, and Text 2 does not discuss extinction.

questions.s:
Text 1
When a famous painting is cleaned, layers of yellowed varnish and old repairs are removed, and colours that viewers have not seen for centuries reappear. Restorers argue that this brings us closer to what the artist actually intended. To them, a cleaned painting is a rediscovered painting, finally free of the dirt of history.

Text 2
Cleaning a painting is never neutral. Some varnishes and glazes removed as "later additions" may have been applied by the artists themselves to soften their colours, and once removed, they cannot be put back. Critics of aggressive restoration argue that the brighter colours revealed may be further from the artist's intention, not closer.

Based on the texts, how would the critics in Text 2 most likely respond to the restorers' argument in Text 1?
o: By warning that cleaning may strip away the artist's own layers and distort the original
By arguing that paintings should be varnished again every few years to protect them
By claiming that most viewers prefer the yellowed colours of paintings left uncleaned
By agreeing that removing old varnish always reveals the colours the artist intended
questions.e: The critics say some removed glazes may be the artist's own, so the cleaned result may be 'further from the artist's intention'. They say nothing about repeated varnishing or viewers' tastes.

questions.s:
Text 1
Historians once explained major events chiefly through the decisions of powerful individuals: kings, generals, revolutionary leaders. In this view, had a single leader chosen differently, the course of history might have changed entirely. Biographies of such figures filled library shelves for generations, while the lives of ordinary people received little attention.

Text 2
No leader acts alone. A general's victory depends on the harvests that feed his army, the roads that carry his supplies and the willingness of thousands of soldiers to follow orders. Yet it would be equally mistaken to treat leaders as mere puppets of such forces; at moments of crisis, one person's choice can tip a balance that conditions have already made fragile.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view described in Text 1?
o: By arguing that ordinary soldiers, rather than leaders, made all of the important decisions
By granting that individuals matter while insisting their choices depend on conditions
By accepting it fully and adding that harvests and roads are of little importance to victory
By rejecting it completely and arguing that individual decisions never change the course of history
questions.e: Text 2 stresses harvests, roads and soldiers, but says treating leaders as 'mere puppets' would be 'equally mistaken', since a choice can tip a fragile balance. That middle position rules out both total rejection and full acceptance.

questions.s:
Text 1
When the city banned thin plastic shopping bags, officials predicted a quick drop in the litter that blocks drains during the monsoon. Shoppers, they said, would soon get used to carrying cloth bags. The ban, they argued, was a simple and cheap way to protect the city's streets and waterways.

Text 2
A year after the ban on plastic bags, a survey of markets found that many shopkeepers were still handing them out. Inspections were rare, fines were small, and cloth bags cost more than many customers wanted to pay. The researchers concluded that a ban without proper enforcement changes very little.

Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the officials' prediction in Text 1?
o: By arguing that plastic bags do not in fact block the city's drains in the monsoon
By claiming that the fines for using plastic bags were too high to be fair
By agreeing that shoppers quickly switched to carrying cloth bags after the ban
By reporting that the weakly enforced ban had less effect than predicted
questions.e: The survey found plastic bags still in use, with rare inspections and small fines, so the predicted quick change did not happen. Text 2 calls the fines small, not too high, and does not dispute that bags block drains.

questions.s:
Text 1
It is widely believed that children learn languages more easily than adults. Young children who move to a new country often speak the local language without an accent within a few years, while their parents may struggle for decades. For this reason, many schools introduce foreign languages as early as possible.

Text 2
In controlled studies, adults often learn the grammar and vocabulary of a new language faster than children, at least at first. Children's advantage appears mainly in pronunciation and in the level they eventually reach after many years of immersion. Whether children learn "more easily," then, depends on what is being measured and over what period.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief described in Text 1?
o: By suggesting that the belief holds for some aspects of learning but not others
By arguing that adults always reach a higher final level in a language than children
By claiming that pronunciation is the only part of a language that really matters
By agreeing that children learn every part of a new language faster than adults do
questions.e: Text 2 gives adults the early lead in grammar and vocabulary but children the edge in pronunciation and final level, so the belief is only partly true. It credits children, not adults, with the higher eventual level.

questions.s:
Text 1
When a computer defeated the world chess champion in 1997, many commentators predicted that people would lose interest in the game. If machines could play better than any human, they asked, why would anyone want to watch humans play? Some even suggested that chess would become a historical curiosity, like a puzzle that had already been solved.

Text 2
Chess is more popular today than at any point in its history, with millions of people playing online every day. Computers have become training partners rather than rivals: young players study engine analysis to learn ideas that once took decades to discover, and viewers of top games follow an engine's evaluation bar to understand who is winning.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the commentators' prediction in Text 1?
o: By claiming that the computer had not really beaten the world champion in 1997
By noting that it has not come true and that computers have helped the game
By arguing that humans can still defeat the strongest chess computers in matches
By agreeing that machines have made human chess much less interesting to watch
questions.e: Text 2 reports record popularity and describes computers as training and viewing aids, the opposite of the predicted decline. It never disputes the 1997 result or claims humans can beat engines.

questions.s:
Text 1
Sending humans to live on Mars, its supporters argue, would protect our species from disasters on Earth, such as an asteroid strike or a global pandemic. A self-sufficient colony would be a backup copy of human civilisation. The cost, though enormous, is small compared with what would be lost if humanity disappeared.

Text 2
Any disaster severe enough to make Earth uninhabitable would still leave it far more habitable than Mars, which has thin air, deadly radiation and no liquid water at its surface. Building shelters on Earth that could survive such events would be cheaper and easier than building a city on another planet. Exploring Mars may be worthwhile for science, but not as an insurance policy.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' argument in Text 1?
o: By claiming that a global pandemic could never make the Earth hard to live on
By arguing that humans should never explore Mars because the planet is so dangerous
By arguing that the same protection could be achieved more easily on Earth
By agreeing that a colony on Mars is the best protection against an asteroid strike
questions.e: Text 2 argues that even a damaged Earth beats Mars and that shelters on Earth would be cheaper, so the backup goal is better met at home. It still calls exploring Mars 'worthwhile for science', which rules out the claim that humans should never go.

questions.s:
Text 1
For a long time, archaeologists believed that farming began in a single region, the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East, and spread outward from there to the rest of the world. Farming, in this view, was one great invention that other peoples copied as they learned of it from their neighbours.

Text 2
Evidence gathered over recent decades shows that farming arose independently in several places, including China, Mesoamerica and the highlands of New Guinea, each with its own crops, from rice and maize to taro. Rather than a single invention, agriculture appears to have been discovered again and again by different peoples.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
o: It agrees with Text 1 but adds that the Fertile Crescent was where rice and maize were first grown.
It challenges the view in Text 1 by presenting evidence of several separate origins.
It supports the view in Text 1 by showing how farming spread outward from one region.
It explains why farming failed to reach China, Mesoamerica and the highlands of New Guinea.
questions.e: Text 1 describes one origin copied elsewhere, while Text 2 reports independent origins with different crops. The crops named belong to those other regions, and farming did develop there.

questions.s:
Text 1
Lahore is growing rapidly, and planners face a choice. Some argue that the city should build upward, allowing tall apartment towers near the centre. Taller buildings, they say, would house more people on less land, protecting farmland at the city's edges and shortening the journeys people make to work each day.

Text 2
Height alone does not make a city dense or efficient. Towers surrounded by car parks and wide roads can house fewer people per hectare than neighbourhoods of four- or five-storey buildings packed along narrow streets, like those of the old walled city. What matters most is how buildings are arranged, not simply how tall they are.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?
o: By arguing that Lahore should stop growing and protect its farmland with strict laws
By claiming that far too many people already live inside the old walled city
By agreeing that only tall towers can protect the farmland at the edges of the city
By questioning whether tall buildings are the best way to reach the density Text 1 wants
questions.e: Text 2 shares the goal of housing many people on little land but argues that layout, not height, achieves it. The walled city is offered as a model of density, not a problem.

questions.s:
Text 1
To understand a poem, a reader must know what its author meant. Letters, diaries and interviews can reveal a poet's intentions, and a reading that contradicts them is simply a misreading. Without such evidence, interpretation becomes guesswork, with each reader inventing whatever meaning happens to suit them. Only the author, after all, knows what the poem was meant to say.

Text 2
Poets are not always the best guides to their own work. Many have admitted that they discovered what a poem meant only after writing it, and some changed their explanations over the years. The words on the page, which every reader can examine, are a firmer basis for interpretation than a poet's private statements, though those statements can still offer useful clues.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that a reading contradicting a poet's intentions is "simply a misreading"?
o: By arguing that the words on the page outweigh the poet's statements
By claiming that every reader's interpretation of a poem is equally valid
By arguing that readers should ignore a poet's letters and interviews completely
By agreeing that letters and diaries are the most reliable guides to what a poem means
questions.e: Text 2 makes 'the words on the page' the firmer basis while granting that poets' statements 'can still offer useful clues'. That concession rules out ignoring them entirely, and preferring the text is not the same as accepting every reading.

questions.s:
Text 1
Pakistan's tree-planting campaigns have put hundreds of millions of saplings in the ground since 2014. Supporters say the programme will cool cities, reduce flooding and absorb carbon dioxide, and they point to the sheer number of trees planted as proof of its success. Officials publish planting totals each year, and every new record is announced as a victory for the environment.

Text 2
Counting saplings says little about a forest. Many young trees die within a year if they are not watered or protected from grazing animals, and trees planted in the wrong places, such as natural grasslands, can harm the ecosystems already there. A better measure of success is how many trees survive, and where they grow.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' evidence in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that planting large numbers of trees always cools cities and reduces floods
By claiming that young trees rarely die once they have been planted in the ground
By arguing that the number of saplings planted is a poor measure of success
By arguing that Pakistan should stop planting trees and protect its grasslands instead
questions.e: Text 2 says counting saplings 'says little' and proposes survival and location as better measures. It warns against planting on grasslands, not against planting altogether, and it says many saplings die.

questions.s:
Text 1
Students who take notes on laptops can type nearly everything a lecturer says, and many assume this makes their notes more useful. A widely cited study, however, found that students who took notes by hand did better on questions requiring understanding. Writing by hand is slower, the researchers argued, which forces students to summarise ideas in their own words.

Text 2
Attempts to repeat the famous note-taking study have produced mixed results. Several found little or no difference between handwritten and typed notes once students had reviewed their notes before the test. What may matter most is not the tool but what students do with it: summarising and reviewing help, whatever the method.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the study described in Text 1?
o: By suggesting its result may not hold and that habits matter more than tools
By arguing that typed notes are always more useful because they are more complete
By agreeing that writing by hand always leads to better understanding than typing
By claiming that reviewing notes before a test makes little difference to results
questions.e: Text 2 reports mixed replications and says reviewing and summarising matter more than the method. It credits reviewing with helping, so it does not dismiss it, and it favours neither tool.

questions.s:
Text 1
Many public libraries charge fines for overdue books. Librarians who support the fines argue that without them, borrowers would keep books for months, leaving other readers waiting. The small charge, they say, reminds people that a library book belongs to everyone, not just to the person who happens to have it.

Text 2
When a city library system abolished overdue fines, most borrowed books still came back on time, and thousands of former members who had stopped visiting because of unpaid fines returned. Fines, the library concluded, had mainly kept the poorest readers away rather than speeding up returns. Staff time once spent chasing small debts now goes to helping readers.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the librarians' argument in Text 1?
o: By claiming that most borrowers would rather buy books than borrow them
By agreeing that borrowers keep books for months whenever no fines are charged
By arguing that libraries should raise their fines to bring back former members
By reporting that removing fines did not cause the long delays they feared
questions.e: In Text 2, books 'still came back on time' after fines ended, contradicting the predicted months-long delays. Members returned because fines were removed, so raising fines would have the opposite effect.

questions.s:
Text 1
Expertise, according to a popular idea, comes from practice: roughly ten thousand hours of it. On this view, talent matters little; almost anyone who practises long and hard enough can reach the top of a field such as music or chess. Stories of famous performers who practised from early childhood are often offered as proof.

Text 2
Practice is essential, but it is not the whole story. In studies of chess players and musicians, the amount of practice explains only part of the differences between performers; some reach expert level with far fewer hours than others. Factors such as the age at which training begins and inborn differences in memory also appear to matter.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the popular idea described in Text 1?
o: By arguing that practice makes no real difference to how skilled a performer becomes
By agreeing that practice matters while denying that it alone explains expertise
By claiming that inborn memory is the only thing that separates experts from others
By agreeing that anyone who practises ten thousand hours will become an expert
questions.e: Text 2 calls practice 'essential' but 'not the whole story', adding age and inborn memory. Memory is one of several factors it mentions, not the only one.

questions.s:
Text 1
Popular films and older history books often show the pyramids of Egypt being built by armies of slaves driven by whips. The image fits a common picture of ancient kings as rulers who could force thousands of people to work for them without any reward or care. Few viewers ever question it.

Text 2
Excavations near the pyramids at Giza have uncovered the remains of workers' villages, with bakeries and cemeteries where labourers were buried with bread and beer for the afterlife. Some skeletons show injuries that had been treated and had healed. Most archaeologists now think the builders were organised, fed and cared for, perhaps as paid workers or as farmers serving in shifts.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
o: It supports the picture in Text 1 with evidence of how harshly the builders were treated.
It argues that the films mentioned in Text 1 are more accurate than older history books.
It presents evidence that challenges the picture of the builders given in Text 1.
It explains how the pyramids were designed, a subject that Text 1 does not discuss.
questions.e: The villages, burials and healed injuries in Text 2 suggest cared-for workers, contradicting Text 1's whipped slaves. The healed injuries show medical care, not harsh treatment, and design is never discussed.

questions.s:
Text 1
Universities should rely less on entrance tests, some educators argue. A single exam, taken on one morning, can be affected by illness, nerves or the coaching that wealthier families can afford. School grades earned over several years, they say, give a fairer picture of a student's ability, since one bad day cannot outweigh years of steady work.

Text 2
School grades have their own problems. Standards differ widely between schools, and some schools award high marks far more generously than others. A common entrance test, whatever its flaws, measures every applicant against the same yardstick, which can help talented students from little-known schools stand out. Abolishing it could hurt the very applicants the educators hope to protect.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the educators' proposal in Text 1?
o: By arguing that grades are unreliable too and that a shared test offers one standard
By claiming that entrance tests are never affected by nerves, illness or private coaching
By arguing that universities should rely only on interviews with each applicant
By agreeing that school grades give the fairest possible picture of a student's ability
questions.e: Text 2 points out that grading standards vary and that a common test uses 'the same yardstick'. It admits the test has flaws, so it does not claim tests are free of nerves or coaching effects.

questions.s:
Text 1
Experienced firefighters, nurses and pilots often make life-or-death decisions in seconds, without consciously weighing their options. Researchers who have studied them argue that such intuition is not mysterious: it is pattern recognition built from years of practice, and in familiar situations it can outperform slow, careful analysis. Training programmes, they suggest, should value such judgment.

Text 2
Intuition deserves trust only in certain conditions. It is reliable when people work in settings that are regular and give quick, clear feedback, as firefighting does. In fields where outcomes are unpredictable and feedback is slow, such as long-term stock-market forecasting, experts' confident hunches are often no better than chance.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the researchers' argument in Text 1?
o: By accepting it fully and adding that stock-market experts also have reliable hunches
By rejecting it and arguing that intuition is no better than chance in firefighting
By accepting it for settings like firefighting while denying it holds in every field
By arguing that slow analysis is always more reliable than intuition in any situation
questions.e: Text 2 names firefighting as a setting where intuition is reliable but says hunches fail where feedback is slow, as in stock forecasting. It reserves 'no better than chance' for those unpredictable fields, not firefighting.

questions.s:
Text 1
Karachi's colonial-era stone buildings, with their carved balconies and arched windows, are disappearing as owners demolish them to build modern towers. Heritage campaigners argue that the city should make it illegal to demolish any building more than a hundred years old. Once such a building is gone, they point out, it can never be replaced.

Text 2
Owners of old buildings in Karachi often have good reasons to sell. Many of the buildings are crumbling, rents are kept at tiny amounts by old agreements, and repairs cost more than the buildings earn. Protecting heritage, these owners argue, will work only if the city also helps pay for upkeep; a ban alone simply leaves buildings to collapse.

Based on the texts, how would the owners in Text 2 most likely respond to the campaigners' proposal in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that banning demolition is the simplest way to protect the city's heritage
By arguing that old buildings have no historical value and should all be replaced
By claiming that the rents charged for old buildings in Karachi are far too high
By arguing that a ban without financial help would fail to save the buildings
questions.e: The owners say 'a ban alone simply leaves buildings to collapse' and ask for help with upkeep. They accept the goal of protecting heritage, and they describe rents as tiny, not too high.

questions.s:
Text 1
Breakfast is often called the most important meal of the day. Many people believe that skipping it leads to weight gain, because those who miss breakfast become so hungry that they overeat later. Advertisements for cereals have repeated this message for decades, and many parents insist that children eat something before school.

Text 2
In a trial in which adults were randomly assigned to eat or skip breakfast for several months, the two groups lost or gained similar amounts of weight. The researchers concluded that, for weight at least, whether a person eats breakfast matters less than what and how much they eat across the whole day.

Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1 that skipping breakfast leads to weight gain?
o: By claiming that what people eat during the day has little effect on their weight
By noting that their trial found no clear weight difference between the groups
By arguing that eating breakfast makes people gain more weight than skipping it
By agreeing that people who skip breakfast tend to overeat later and gain weight
questions.e: Both groups' weight changed similarly, so the trial gives no support for the belief. The researchers stress that daily food intake matters, the opposite of saying daily intake has little effect.

questions.s:
Text 1
Computer programs can now produce paintings in the style of famous artists within seconds. Some critics insist that such images cannot be art, because art requires a human being with something to express. A machine, they argue, has no experiences, no feelings and therefore nothing to say. However pleasing the result, it is decoration rather than art.

Text 2
Whether a machine "means" anything may matter less than it seems. People write the instructions, select among hundreds of results and decide which images to show. Photography faced a similar objection in the nineteenth century, when critics claimed that a camera merely copied the world; today few would deny that a great photograph can be art.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critics' argument in Text 1?
o: By claiming that photography is still not accepted as a form of art by critics
By suggesting that the people guiding the program may supply the expression needed
By arguing that machines have experiences and feelings of their own to express
By agreeing that images made with a computer can never be considered works of art
questions.e: Text 2 shifts attention to the human choices behind the images and compares the case to photography, which is now accepted as art. It does not claim machines have feelings; it says their lack may 'matter less than it seems'.

questions.s:
Text 1
Children should first learn to read in the language they speak at home, many educators argue. A child in rural Sindh who speaks Sindhi at home but is taught to read in English must learn a new language and a new skill at the same time, and many fall behind. Reading skills learned in a familiar language, they add, transfer readily to a second one.

Text 2
Parents in many parts of Pakistan want their children taught in English from the start, believing it offers the best chance of a good job. Their concern is understandable. Yet studies from several countries suggest that children taught first in their home language often end up reading English better than those taught in English from the beginning.

Based on the texts, how would the educators in Text 1 most likely respond to the parents described in Text 2?
o: By arguing that children in rural Sindh do not need to learn English at all
By claiming that Urdu is more useful than English for finding a good job
By arguing that starting with the home language may best serve their goal
By agreeing that children should be taught to read in English from their first day
questions.e: The educators believe reading skills transfer to a second language, which fits Text 2's finding that home-language starters often read English better. So they would say the parents' aim, strong English, is best reached that way; they never reject English itself.

questions.s:
Text 1
Several countries have banned mobile phones in schools, and supporters report calmer classrooms, fewer distractions and less online bullying during the school day. Teachers say pupils talk to one another more at break time instead of staring at screens. In the supporters' view, the benefits are so obvious that no further evidence is needed.

Text 2
Studies of phone bans have found mixed effects on test scores: some schools improved, others saw no change. A ban may also remove a useful tool, since phones can be used for research or language apps when teachers plan for them. Clear rules about when phones may be used, rather than a total ban, may offer the benefits without the losses.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' view in Text 1?
o: By claiming that online bullying has increased in schools that have banned phones
By arguing that phones cause no distraction at all in modern school classrooms
By agreeing that phone bans have clearly raised pupils' test scores in every school
By suggesting that a total ban may not be needed to gain its benefits
