questions.e: Text 2 reports mixed results and proposes clear rules that 'may offer the benefits without the losses'. It says some schools saw no change in scores, so it does not claim bans raised scores everywhere.

questions.s:
Text 1
Wind turbines are often criticised for killing birds. Opponents of new wind farms along the coast of Sindh point to images of birds struck by spinning blades and argue that the turbines pose an unacceptable threat to wildlife, especially to the migrating species that pass through the region each winter.

Text 2
Turbines do kill birds, but the numbers need context. Studies in several countries have found that far more birds die from collisions with buildings, from cats and from power lines than from wind turbines. Careful siting, away from major migration routes, can reduce the risk further. Fossil-fuel power, meanwhile, harms birds through pollution and climate change.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the opponents' argument in Text 1?
o: By accepting that turbines kill birds while arguing that the threat is relatively small
By agreeing that wind turbines are the most serious danger facing migrating birds
By denying that wind turbines are responsible for the deaths of any birds at all
By arguing that new wind farms should be built directly on major migration routes
questions.e: Text 2 begins 'Turbines do kill birds' but compares them with larger causes such as buildings and cats. It recommends siting turbines away from migration routes, not on them.

questions.s:
Text 1
Pakistani schools are often criticised for relying on rote learning. Students memorise answers word for word, critics say, and can repeat definitions without understanding them. Such a system, they argue, produces graduates who struggle with unfamiliar problems. Examinations that reward exact repetition only make the problem worse, since teachers naturally teach to the test.

Text 2
Memorisation has a poor reputation, but it is not the enemy of understanding. Fluent recall of basic facts, such as multiplication tables or key vocabulary, frees the mind to think about harder problems. The trouble arises when memorising becomes the only goal, and students are never asked to use what they have learned.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critics in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that rote learning alone is harmful while defending some memorisation
By agreeing that memorising multiplication tables stops students from understanding
By claiming that Pakistani examinations already reward understanding over recall
By arguing that students should never be asked to memorise facts or definitions
questions.e: Text 2 defends recall of basic facts but locates 'the trouble' where memorising is the only goal, which matches part of the critics' concern. It praises learning tables, so it does not see them as a barrier to understanding.

questions.s:
Text 1
Bans on plastic straws have spread to cafés and cities around the world. Supporters say that straws, which are used for a few minutes and then thrown away, are an easy place to start cutting plastic waste, and that a visible ban encourages people to think about plastic in general.

Text 2
Plastic straws make up only a tiny fraction of the plastic that reaches the oceans; abandoned fishing nets and other gear make up a far larger share of the plastic floating at sea. Focusing on straws, critics worry, may let governments and companies appear active while the largest sources of ocean plastic go unaddressed.

Based on the texts, how would the critics in Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' reasoning in Text 1?
o: By claiming that fishing gear makes up only a tiny share of the plastic in the oceans
By agreeing that straws are the main source of the plastic that reaches the oceans
By arguing that plastic straws should be encouraged because they are so convenient
By warning that a focus on straws may distract from much larger sources of pollution
questions.e: The critics say straws are a 'tiny fraction' and fear the bans let larger sources such as fishing gear go unaddressed. They describe fishing gear, not straws, as the larger share.

questions.s:
Text 1
Historical novelists, some readers complain, take too many liberties. When a novel invents conversations between real Mughal emperors or changes the order of battles, readers who know little history may come away believing things that never happened. A novelist who writes about real people, these readers argue, owes them accuracy.

Text 2
A historical novel is not a history book, and readers generally know it. Its task is to imagine what the past felt like from inside: what a servant feared or a prince desired. Inventing dialogue is unavoidable, since no record preserves most conversations. Changing well-documented facts is another matter, however, and a good novelist explains such changes in an author's note.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the readers' complaint in Text 1?
o: By rejecting it entirely, since novelists may change any historical fact they like
By arguing that readers of historical novels usually believe everything they read
By defending invented dialogue while saying changed facts need explaining
By accepting it entirely, since novelists should never invent conversations for real people
questions.e: Text 2 calls invented dialogue 'unavoidable' but treats changing documented facts as 'another matter' that needs an author's note. It thus splits the complaint, answering one part and partly accepting the other, and it says readers 'generally know' a novel is not history.

questions.s:
Text 1
Few people cycle to work in Lahore, and city officials say the reason is simple: residents prefer the comfort of cars and motorcycles. Building cycle lanes, they argue, would waste money on roads that almost no one would use. The heat of the summer months, they add, makes cycling unattractive for much of the year.

Text 2
In cities that have built safe, connected cycle lanes, the number of cyclists has often risen sharply within a few years. Surveys suggest that many people would cycle if they did not fear sharing roads with fast traffic. Low numbers of cyclists today may reflect dangerous roads more than people's preferences.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the officials' argument in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that the residents of Lahore will always prefer cars and motorcycles
By suggesting that few people cycle because the roads feel unsafe
By arguing that the summer heat in Lahore makes cycling dangerous to people's health
By claiming that cycle lanes are too expensive for most cities to build and maintain
questions.e: Text 2 says low cycling 'may reflect dangerous roads more than people's preferences', directly challenging the officials' explanation. It does not discuss heat or cost.

questions.s:
Text 1
Woolly mammoths disappeared from most of their range around ten thousand years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age. Many scientists blame the changing climate: as the cold grasslands on which mammoths fed gave way to forests and wetlands, their food supply shrank and their populations collapsed, leaving only small groups on remote islands.

Text 2
Mammoths had survived earlier warm periods, which suggests that climate alone may not explain their disappearance. Their decline also coincided with the spread of human hunters across northern Europe, Asia and the Americas. Many researchers now think that a combination of shrinking habitat and hunting, rather than either factor alone, pushed mammoth populations past the point of recovery.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that climate change alone fully explains why the mammoths disappeared
By arguing that climate change was probably one cause among others
By rejecting the idea that the climate changed at the end of the last Ice Age
By claiming that human hunters were the only cause of the mammoths' extinction
questions.e: Text 2 keeps shrinking habitat as a factor but adds hunting, 'rather than either factor alone'. That rules out both 'climate alone' and 'hunters were the only cause'.

questions.s:
Text 1
Tourism has brought new income to valleys such as Hunza and Swat. Families who once relied only on farming now run guest houses, restaurants and jeep services, and many young people no longer need to leave for the cities to find work. Local shops now stock goods that were hard to find a decade ago.

Text 2
The boom in tourism has had costs that visitors rarely see. In some valleys, hotels have been built on riverbanks prone to flooding, rubbish left by visitors piles up on mountain trails, and the price of land has risen beyond the reach of local families. Without planning, residents warn, tourism could damage the very landscapes that attract it.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
o: It explains why many young people from the valleys are still moving to the cities.
It rejects the claim in Text 1 that tourism has brought any new income to the valleys.
It provides further examples of the economic benefits that Text 1 has described.
It points to drawbacks of a development whose benefits Text 1 describes.
questions.e: Text 1 lists tourism's economic gains, and Text 2 describes hidden costs such as flood-prone hotels, litter and land prices. Text 2 never denies the new income; it adds what that income has cost.

questions.s:
Text 1
Reading literary fiction, some psychologists claim, makes people more empathetic. In one study, participants who read a short literary story scored higher on a test of recognising others' emotions than participants who read non-fiction or nothing at all. Fiction, the researchers suggested, trains readers to imagine the minds of others.

Text 2
Later attempts to repeat that study often failed to find the same short-term effect. Yet surveys consistently show that people who read a great deal of fiction over their lives tend to score higher on measures of empathy. Whether reading causes empathy, or empathetic people simply enjoy fiction more, remains unclear.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
o: By arguing that readers of fiction are in fact less empathetic than other people
By agreeing that a single literary story reliably makes its readers more empathetic
By noting that a link exists but that its direction of cause is uncertain
By claiming that the surveys prove that reading fiction makes people more empathetic
questions.e: Text 2 reports failed replications but a consistent link in surveys, then says it is unclear whether reading causes empathy or the reverse. The surveys show an association, which is exactly why Text 2 does not treat them as proof.

questions.s:
Text 1
Competitive video gaming, or e-sports, now fills stadiums and offers prize money in the millions. Its fans argue that it should be recognised as a sport: top players train for hours each day, work in teams and need lightning-fast reactions. Some international sporting events have even begun to include it.

Text 2
Whatever the skill involved, e-sports lack the physical exertion that most definitions of sport require. Chess also demands training and quick thinking, and is sometimes played in teams, yet few people call it a sport in the same sense as football or athletics. E-sports, on this view, are better described as competitive games.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the fans' argument in Text 1?
o: By arguing that skill and training are not enough without physical effort
By arguing that e-sports players need no real skill or training in order to succeed
By claiming that chess requires more physical exertion than football or athletics do
By agreeing that e-sports should count as sports because their players train so hard
questions.e: Text 2 grants the skill ('Whatever the skill involved') but says sport requires physical exertion, using chess as a parallel. It never denies that players are skilled.

questions.s:
Text 1
School uniforms, their supporters argue, reduce competition over clothes. When every pupil wears the same shirt and trousers, children from poorer families are less likely to be teased, and parents are spared the cost of buying fashionable outfits. Uniforms also give pupils a sense of belonging to their school and to one another.

Text 2
Uniforms can be surprisingly expensive. Many schools require blazers, ties and badges bought only from a single approved shop, which often charges far more than ordinary clothing stores. For poorer families, these costs can outweigh any savings on everyday clothes, especially when growing children outgrow their uniforms every single year.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' claim in Text 1 about cost?
o: By pointing out that uniforms themselves can be costly for poorer families
By arguing that children from poorer families are teased more when wearing uniforms
By agreeing that uniforms always save families money on their children's clothing
By claiming that approved shops sell uniforms more cheaply than other clothing stores
questions.e: Text 2 says approved-shop prices can 'outweigh any savings', answering the claim that uniforms spare parents expense. It says those shops charge more, not less, and it does not discuss teasing.

questions.s:
Text 1
Urban beekeeping has become popular in many cities, and supporters present it as a way to help pollinators. Rooftop hives, they say, give bees a refuge from the pesticides of the countryside and help reverse the decline of bee populations. Many companies now place hives on office roofs as a sign of their concern for nature.

Text 2
Honeybees are farmed animals, not endangered wildlife, and adding hives to a city can harm the wild bees that are actually in decline. Honeybees compete with wild species for the same flowers, and in some cities with many hives, researchers have found fewer wild bees. Planting more flowers would help pollinators more than adding hives.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the supporters' view in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that rooftop hives are the best way to reverse the decline of bees
By claiming that wild bees compete with honeybees for space on city rooftops
By arguing that adding hives may harm the wild bees most in need of help
By arguing that pesticides in the countryside pose no threat to bees of any kind
questions.e: Text 2 says honeybees are not the declining species and compete with wild bees for flowers, so more hives can hurt the bees that need help. The competition is for flowers, not rooftop space, and pesticides are not discussed.

questions.s:
Text 1
Cheap, fashionable clothing has made it possible for more people than ever to dress well. Shoppers who once owned a few outfits can now buy new styles every season at low prices, and clothing factories have created millions of jobs in countries such as Bangladesh and Pakistan. For many young women there, a factory wage is their first independent income.

Text 2
The low price of fast fashion hides its real cost. Garments are often worn only a few times before being thrown away, and producing them uses large amounts of water and dye that can pollute rivers near factories. Many factory workers, too, earn low wages in difficult and sometimes dangerous conditions.

Which choice best describes a difference between the two texts?
o: Text 1 criticises shoppers, while Text 2 criticises the governments of factory countries.
Text 1 discusses clothing made in Bangladesh, while Text 2 discusses clothing made in Europe.
Text 1 stresses the pollution from factories, while Text 2 stresses the jobs they create.
Text 1 stresses the benefits of cheap clothing, while Text 2 stresses its hidden costs.
questions.e: Text 1 praises low prices and new jobs; Text 2 turns to waste, pollution and low wages. The option giving Text 1 pollution and Text 2 jobs swaps the two texts' points.

questions.s:
Text 1
Every child should learn to write computer code, some educators say. Coding teaches logical thinking, and in a world run by software, students who cannot code will be at a disadvantage in the job market. Several countries have already made it a required school subject, often starting in the first years of primary school.

Text 2
Teaching coding to every pupil assumes that today's programming skills will still be needed when they start work. Yet tools that write code automatically are improving quickly. What may last longer is the ability to break problems into steps and check whether a solution works, skills that can be taught through mathematics and science as well as through coding.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the educators' proposal in Text 1?
o: By arguing that logical thinking is no longer a useful skill for most students
By suggesting the lasting value lies in problem-solving skills, not coding as such
By claiming that mathematics and science should be removed from school timetables
By agreeing that every child must learn to code in order to find a good job
questions.e: Text 2 doubts that specific coding skills will last but values breaking problems into steps, which other subjects can teach too. It values logical thinking rather than dismissing it, and it names mathematics and science as ways to teach it.

questions.s:
Text 1
For a long time, archaeologists regarded art as a sign of the uniquely modern human mind. Neanderthals, in this view, were capable hunters but lacked the imagination needed to create symbols or decorate objects. The painted caves of France and Spain were credited entirely to our own species, Homo sapiens.

Text 2
Red pigment markings in caves in Spain have been dated to more than 64,000 years ago, before modern humans are thought to have reached the region. If the dates are correct, the markings were made by Neanderthals. Some researchers question the dating method, but if it holds, the line between Neanderthal and modern human minds may be less sharp than once believed.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view described in Text 1?
o: By suggesting that new evidence may challenge it, if the dating holds
By stating that the view has been conclusively disproved by the discoveries in Spain
By arguing that modern humans made the Spanish markings before Neanderthals arrived
By agreeing that Neanderthals lacked the imagination needed to create any symbols
questions.e: Text 2 says the markings would be Neanderthal 'if the dates are correct' and notes doubts about the method, so it challenges the view only conditionally. 'Conclusively disproved' ignores those repeated 'if' clauses.

questions.s:
Text 1
Bottled water is often marketed as purer and healthier than tap water. Many families in Pakistani cities buy it for drinking, believing that the water from their taps is unsafe. Sales of bottled water have risen steadily for years, and new brands appear on shop shelves almost every single month.

Text 2
In many cities, tap water is in fact contaminated, often because old pipes leak and allow sewage to seep in. Bottled water is a reasonable choice for families in such places. But some brands of bottled water have themselves failed quality tests, and boiling tap water is a cheaper way to make it safer to drink.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the families' belief in Text 1?
o: By claiming that every brand of bottled water has failed official quality tests
By arguing that tap water in Pakistani cities is always clean and safe to drink
By agreeing their tap water may be unsafe but noting bottled water can fail too
By arguing that boiling tap water makes it more dangerous than bottled water
questions.e: Text 2 confirms that tap water is often contaminated but warns that 'some brands' of bottled water have failed tests. 'Some brands' is not every brand, and boiling is offered as a cheaper way to make water safer.

questions.s:
Text 1
Museums should charge no entry fee, many campaigners argue. Culture belongs to everyone, and even a small fee keeps away families with little money. When some national museums abroad stopped charging, visitor numbers rose sharply. A museum that charges for entry, the campaigners say, is a museum for the wealthy.

Text 2
Free entry does raise visitor numbers, but studies suggest that most of the extra visitors are people who already visited museums often, rather than new visitors from poorer backgrounds. Reaching those families may require other steps, such as school trips, events in local languages and exhibitions about their own communities.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the campaigners' argument in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that free entry alone will bring families with little money to museums
By granting that free entry raises numbers while doubting it reaches poorer families
By arguing that museums should raise their fees to pay for school trips and events
By denying that removing entry fees increases the number of people visiting museums
questions.e: Text 2 accepts the rise in visitors but says most are existing museum-goers, so other steps are needed to reach poorer families. It does not deny the rise or suggest higher fees.

questions.s:
Text 1
Large dams on the Indus and its tributaries supply a significant share of Pakistan's electricity and store water for farming. Supporters of new dams argue that more storage is urgently needed, since the country can hold only a small fraction of its yearly river flow, and much of the monsoon water runs unused to the sea.

Text 2
Large dams bring benefits but also lasting problems. Their reservoirs gradually fill with silt, reducing storage, and the reduced flow of water and sediment downstream has contributed to the shrinking of the Indus delta, where seawater now pushes further inland. Any plan for new dams, critics say, must account for these costs.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
o: It rejects the claim in Text 1 that dams store water and produce electricity.
It provides more evidence that new dams are urgently needed across Pakistan.
It explains how the turbines inside a large dam produce electricity.
It raises costs that should be weighed against the benefits described in Text 1.
questions.e: Text 2 opens by granting that dams 'bring benefits' and then adds silting and delta loss as costs to weigh. It accepts, rather than rejects, Text 1's points about storage and power.

questions.s:
Text 1
Some popular books describe forests as communities in which trees "talk" to one another, sharing food with their young and warning neighbours of danger through underground fungal networks. In this picture, a forest is less a collection of competitors than a cooperative family in which older trees care for younger ones.

Text 2
Fungal networks linking tree roots are real, and some chemicals do pass between trees through them. But recent reviews argue that the evidence for trees deliberately sharing food or sending warnings is weak, and that many field studies have been overstated in popular accounts. The fungi may simply be serving their own interests, trading nutrients for sugar.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the picture of forests in Text 1?
o: By denying that fungal networks connect the roots of different trees at all
By accepting that the networks exist while doubting that trees use them to cooperate
By arguing that trees compete with fungi for nutrients more than with each other
By agreeing that trees share food with their young through fungal networks
questions.e: Text 2 says the networks 'are real' but calls the evidence for deliberate sharing and warning 'weak'. It suggests the fungi trade nutrients for their own benefit; it does not describe trees competing with fungi.

questions.s:
Text 1
Money, a famous study suggested, buys happiness only up to a point. Once people earned enough to cover their basic needs and some comforts, further increases in income made little difference to how happy they said they felt from day to day. The finding was widely reported as proof that chasing a higher salary is pointless.

Text 2
A more recent study, which asked people about their feelings many times a day, found that happiness kept rising with income well beyond the earlier limit, at least for most people. Only among the unhappiest group did the effect level off. The two studies may differ less than they seem: money appears to help most people, but it cannot cure every kind of unhappiness.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the finding described in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that income stops affecting happiness for everyone above a certain level
By claiming that the unhappiest people gain the most happiness from higher incomes
By suggesting that it holds mainly for an unhappy minority, not for most people
By arguing that money has no effect at all on how happy most people feel each day
questions.e: Text 2 finds happiness rising with income for most people and levelling off 'only among the unhappiest group', which is where the earlier limit seems to apply. It says the effect levels off for the unhappiest, so they gain least, not most.

questions.s:
Text 1
Many young Pakistanis now write Urdu in the Roman alphabet when texting, and some commentators fear this will weaken the Urdu script. If people grow used to typing "kya haal hai" in Roman letters, they argue, fewer will bother to read and write in Nastaliq, and a rich written tradition will slowly fade.

Text 2
Roman Urdu on phones may reflect convenience rather than a rejection of the script. Early mobile keyboards did not support Urdu well, so people adapted. Now that Urdu keyboards are widely available, some surveys suggest that younger users switch between scripts depending on the situation, using Roman letters for quick messages and Urdu script for more formal writing.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the commentators' fear in Text 1?
o: By suggesting the habit is practical and need not mean the script is abandoned
By claiming that Urdu keyboards are still unavailable on most mobile phones
By agreeing that Roman Urdu will soon replace the Urdu script in formal writing
By arguing that young Pakistanis should stop sending text messages in Urdu
questions.e: Text 2 explains Roman Urdu as a response to old keyboards and reports users keeping Urdu script for formal writing. It says Urdu keyboards are now 'widely available', the reverse of saying they are still unavailable.

questions.s:
Text 1
Several companies that tested a four-day working week reported that employees were less tired and more focused, and that the amount of work completed hardly fell. Managers at these firms say the shorter week has made it easier to keep good staff, and some have decided to keep it permanently.

Text 2
Results from four-day week trials should be read with care. Most companies that took part chose to do so, and many were office-based firms whose work could be reorganised easily. Hospitals, factories and shops, where someone must be present for every hour of opening, may find the change far harder to make.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the results reported in Text 1?
o: By agreeing that every business could easily move to a four-day working week
By arguing that the companies' employees were in fact more tired than before
By claiming that hospitals and factories already work only four days a week
By warning that the results may not apply to every kind of workplace
questions.e: Text 2 notes that the firms chose to take part and were mostly offices, so the results may not carry over to hospitals or shops. It does not dispute the reported results themselves.

questions.s:
Text 1
Automation, some economists warn, will soon eliminate millions of jobs. Self-driving trucks, automated checkouts and software that writes reports could replace drivers, cashiers and clerks within a generation, leaving many workers with no obvious place in the economy. Unlike earlier machines, which replaced muscle, these technologies replace judgment, and the warning is that this time few new jobs will appear to absorb those displaced.

Text 2
Similar warnings have accompanied almost every new technology since the power loom, and yet total employment has generally grown over time as new kinds of work appeared. This history does not guarantee a smooth future, however. New jobs often require different skills and appear in different places, and the workers who lose old jobs are rarely the ones who fill the new ones.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the economists' warning in Text 1?
o: By arguing that history guarantees that every worker who loses a job will find a new one
By agreeing that automation will leave millions with no place in the economy
By doubting that work will vanish overall while granting that many may still suffer
By claiming that new technologies have always reduced the total number of jobs
questions.e: Text 2 cites history to suggest total employment will grow, but warns that displaced workers rarely get the new jobs. It says history 'does not guarantee a smooth future', ruling out a guarantee for every worker.

questions.s:
Text 1
The Library of Alexandria is often said to have been destroyed in a single great fire, taking with it much of the learning of the ancient world. The story has made the library a symbol of how quickly knowledge can be lost. Paintings and films have often shown flames consuming its shelves of scrolls.

Text 2
Most historians now think the Library of Alexandria declined slowly over several centuries. Funding fell, scholars were expelled during political conflicts, and papyrus scrolls that were not regularly copied simply decayed. A fire in 48 BCE may have damaged part of the collection, but no single event destroyed it. Its end was quiet neglect rather than catastrophe.

Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
o: It argues that the Library of Alexandria never existed in the ancient world.
It explains why papyrus scrolls last longer than books printed on paper.
It confirms the account in Text 1 by giving the date of the single great fire.
It offers a more gradual account of the loss described in Text 1.
questions.e: Text 1 describes sudden destruction by fire, while Text 2 describes slow decline over centuries and says 'no single event destroyed it'. The fire of 48 BCE is mentioned only as partial damage, not as confirmation.

questions.s:
Text 1
Organic farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides, is often presented as the future of agriculture. Its supporters point out that organic farms tend to have healthier soils and more wildlife than conventional farms. Some argue that all farms should eventually switch to organic methods, which they see as kinder to both people and the land.

Text 2
On average, organic farms produce smaller harvests than conventional ones growing the same crops, though the gap varies widely between crops and regions. Feeding a growing population entirely through organic methods could therefore require more farmland, possibly at the expense of forests. Combining the best organic practices with careful use of fertilisers may be a more realistic path.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view in Text 1 that organic farming is the future of agriculture?
o: By noting that lower yields could make a complete switch costly to forests
By denying that organic farms have healthier soils or more wildlife than others
By arguing that conventional farms always produce smaller harvests than organic ones
By agreeing that every farm should switch to organic methods as soon as possible
questions.e: Text 2 says organic farms average smaller harvests, so going fully organic could require clearing forests, and it proposes a mixed approach. It never disputes the soil and wildlife benefits, and it says conventional harvests are larger.

questions.s:
Terraced fields in the Hunza valley are often seen as a sign of how hard farming is in the mountains. Yet the terraces also make farming possible there at all. By turning steep slopes into flat steps, they slow the meltwater that runs down from glaciers, keep thin soil from washing away and let farmers grow apricots, potatoes and wheat on land that would otherwise be bare rock.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Glacial meltwater in Hunza is now too scarce to support terraced farming.
Hunza's farmers prefer apricots to every other crop that the valley's soil could support.
Hunza's terraces are what allow crops to be grown on otherwise unusable slopes.
Terraced fields are harder to farm than flat fields in the plains of Punjab.
questions.e: The text grants that terraces suggest hardship but stresses that they make mountain farming possible by holding water and soil. The text lists apricots only as one crop and never ranks them, so the apricot option turns a detail into a claim the text does not make.

questions.s:
When the novelist Rafia Siddiqui began writing her second book, she kept a notebook of overheard conversations from Karachi's buses and tea stalls. She did not copy the talk directly into her chapters. Instead, she studied the rhythm of the speech, the way people interrupted each other and the jokes they repeated, so that her invented characters would sound as though they belonged to the city.

According to the text, why did Siddiqui keep a notebook of overheard conversations?
o: To learn how real speech sounded so that her characters' dialogue would feel authentic
To collect true stories that she could retell word for word in her second novel
To record jokes that she planned to publish later as a separate collection
To prove to her publisher that she had carefully researched Karachi's public transport system
questions.e: The text says she studied rhythm, interruptions and jokes so her characters would sound as if they belonged to Karachi. The option about retelling stories word for word contradicts the statement that she did not copy the talk directly.

questions.s:
For decades, historians described the Mughal emperor Akbar's court as a place where policy was set by the emperor alone. Recent work on court records paints a more crowded picture. Letters, petitions and account books show revenue officers, provincial governors and even merchants shaping decisions on taxes and trade routes, often by supplying information the emperor could not have gathered himself.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Merchants held more power than provincial governors in Akbar's empire.
Akbar's court records were deliberately hidden from historians until very recently.
Akbar personally gathered all the information he needed to set taxes.
New evidence suggests that many people besides Akbar influenced decisions at his court.
questions.e: The text contrasts the older view of Akbar ruling alone with records showing officers, governors and merchants shaping policy. Nothing compares merchants with governors, so that option invents a ranking the text never gives.

questions.s:
Octopuses can change colour in a fraction of a second, but most species are thought to be colour-blind. Marine biologist Hana Okafor suggests that the animal's skin may solve the puzzle. She found that octopus skin contains light-sensitive proteins similar to those in eyes, which could allow the skin itself to detect the colours around it and help the animal match its surroundings without seeing them.

Based on the text, what puzzle does Okafor's finding attempt to explain?
o: Why octopuses change colour more slowly than most other camouflaging animals
How an animal that probably cannot see colour manages to match the colours around it
How octopuses learned to see colour after millions of years of colour-blindness
Why the light-sensitive proteins in octopus eyes differ from those found in octopus skin
questions.e: The puzzle is that octopuses change colour to match surroundings though most are colour-blind; light-sensitive skin could explain it. The option about learning to see colour contradicts the text, which says they are still thought to be colour-blind.

questions.s:
Many small shops in Lahore once relied only on cash. Over the past few years, a large share of them have begun accepting payments through mobile wallets. Shopkeepers interviewed in a 2023 survey gave a practical reason: customers increasingly arrived without cash, and shops that refused digital payments lost sales to neighbours that accepted them. Few shopkeepers said they had switched because they trusted the technology more than cash.

According to the text, what was the main reason shopkeepers began accepting mobile wallet payments?
o: Mobile wallets charged lower fees than banks did for card payments.
The government required all shops to accept digital payments.
They wanted to avoid losing customers who no longer carried cash.
They had come to trust digital technology more than paper money.
questions.e: The survey reason is that customers came without cash and shops refusing digital payments lost sales. The trust option is tempting but the text says few shopkeepers gave that reason.

questions.s:
The architect Nayyar Ali Dada is often praised for the red brick of his Lahore buildings, and critics usually treat the material as a nod to Mughal tradition. Dada's own notes suggest a further motive. Brick, he wrote, could be made and laid by local craftsmen without imported machines, which kept costs down and kept skilled work in the city. For him, tradition and practicality pointed the same way.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Dada rejected imported machines because he distrusted modern building methods.
Dada's use of brick reflected practical concerns as well as respect for tradition.
Critics have been wrong to link Dada's brickwork to Mughal architecture.
Local craftsmen persuaded Dada to abandon his earlier plans for large concrete buildings.
questions.e: The text adds a practical motive (local labour, lower cost) to the traditional one, concluding that both 'pointed the same way'. The option saying critics were wrong overstates it: the text calls the practical reason 'a further motive', not a replacement.

questions.s:
Honeybees communicate the location of food through the 'waggle dance'. A forager returning to the hive moves in a figure-of-eight pattern, and the direction of the straight middle run tells other bees which way to fly relative to the sun. The longer the bee waggles during that run, the farther away the food is.

According to the text, what does the length of the waggle run indicate?
o: How far the food is from the hive
How much food the forager found
Which direction the food lies in
What kind of flower the food came from
questions.e: The text states that the longer the waggle, the farther away the food. Direction is shown by the angle of the run, not its length, so that option confuses the two signals.

questions.s:
In 1999, a small school in rural Sindh started lending its library books to families for a whole week instead of a single day. Teachers had worried that books would be lost. Instead, the share of books returned stayed almost the same, and parents began asking for titles they could read aloud to younger children. Within two years, younger siblings of pupils were arriving at school already able to recognise letters.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Teachers in rural Sindh were right to fear that lent books would be lost.
Parents in rural Sindh preferred reading aloud at home to sending their young children to school.
The school stopped lending books after younger children learned their letters.
Longer book loans at one school led to more reading at home without many lost books.
questions.e: The text reports that returns stayed steady while home reading grew and siblings arrived knowing letters. The option about teachers being right contradicts the result that the return rate barely changed.

questions.s:
Economists long assumed that people who win small prizes in lotteries simply spend the money. A study of 4,000 winners in several countries found something subtler. Winners who received their prize as a single payment did spend most of it within months, but those paid in monthly instalments were far more likely to save part of each payment. The form of the windfall, the researchers concluded, shapes behaviour as much as its size.

Based on the text, what did the study suggest about lottery winners?
o: Most winners saved their prizes regardless of how they were paid.
Winners of larger prizes saved more than winners of smaller prizes.
Monthly payments caused winners to spend their money more quickly.
Whether they saved depended partly on how their prize was paid out.
questions.e: Single-payment winners spent quickly while instalment winners saved more, so the payment form mattered. The option about prize size is tempting because size is mentioned, but the study compared payment forms, not prize amounts.

questions.s:
Bamboo is sometimes called a 'green steel' because, weight for weight, some species are as strong in tension as mild steel. Engineers in several Asian countries now use it for scaffolding and low-rise houses. Its weakness is not strength but durability: untreated bamboo is attacked by insects and fungi within a few years, so builders must soak or heat-treat it before use.

According to the text, what is the main drawback of bamboo as a building material?
o: It can only be grown in a few Asian countries with wet climates.
It is much weaker in tension than mild steel of the same weight.
Unless it is treated, it decays and is damaged by pests fairly quickly.
It is too heavy to be used safely for scaffolding on tall city buildings.
questions.e: The text says bamboo's weakness 'is not strength but durability': insects and fungi attack it unless treated. The tension option reverses the text, which compares some species favourably with steel.

questions.s:
The poet Parveen Shakir wrote mostly in the ghazal, a form with strict rules of rhyme and metre that had been shaped for centuries largely by male poets. Rather than abandoning the form, Shakir used it to describe experiences rarely given voice in it before, such as a woman's view of love, marriage and independence. Readers found the familiar form made her new subjects feel all the more striking.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Shakir's readers disliked the subjects she chose for her poems.
Shakir was the first poet to write ghazals in the Urdu language.
Shakir brought new perspectives into a traditional poetic form.
Shakir rejected the ghazal because its rules were too strict.
questions.e: The text says Shakir kept the ghazal but used it for a woman's perspective, which readers found striking. The option that she rejected the form contradicts 'Rather than abandoning the form'.

questions.s:
A city's trees are often valued for shade and beauty, but a team studying Islamabad found another effect. Streets with continuous tree cover were up to 4 °C cooler on summer afternoons than nearby streets without it, and households on the shaded streets used noticeably less electricity for air-conditioning. The team cautioned, however, that scattered single trees produced almost none of this benefit; the cooling came from canopies that joined above the road.

According to the text, what condition was needed for trees to reduce street temperatures?
o: The trees had to be planted close to houses with air-conditioners.
The trees had to be spread out singly along both sides of the road.
The trees had to be of species that grow well in Islamabad's climate.
The trees had to form a continuous canopy over the street.
questions.e: The team found the cooling came from canopies that joined above the road and that scattered single trees gave almost no benefit. The option about single trees on both sides is the opposite of that finding.

questions.s:
Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air. Whales take advantage of this: some species produce low-frequency calls that can be detected by other whales hundreds of kilometres away. Researchers worry that noise from ships, which also falls in low frequencies, may be shrinking the distance over which whales can hear one another.

Based on the text, why are researchers concerned about ship noise?
o: It travels more slowly in water than whale calls do.
It may interfere with the long-distance calls whales use to communicate.
It causes whales to swim towards busy shipping lanes in search of company.
It raises the frequency of the calls that whales produce.
questions.e: Ship noise shares the low frequencies of whale calls and may reduce how far whales can hear each other. The option about frequency is tempting but the text never says whales change the pitch of their calls.

questions.s:
In the 1950s, the Pakistani physicist Abdus Salam began working on the idea that two of nature's basic forces, electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force, might be different faces of a single force. The idea was mathematically demanding and many colleagues doubted it. Experiments in the 1970s confirmed key predictions of the theory, and in 1979 Salam shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for his part in it.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Salam's doubtful colleagues eventually convinced him to give up a mathematically difficult idea.
Salam carried out the 1970s experiments himself before winning the prize.
Salam proved that electromagnetism is stronger than the weak nuclear force.
An idea Salam pursued despite doubts was later supported by experiments and honoured.
questions.e: The text moves from Salam's doubted idea to its experimental confirmation and the 1979 Nobel Prize. It never says Salam ran the experiments, so that option adds an unsupported detail.

questions.s:
Many people think deserts are always hot, but the Gobi Desert in Mongolia and China has some of the coldest winters of any desert on Earth. Temperatures there can fall below −30 °C. What makes the Gobi a desert is not heat but how little rain and snow it receives each year.

According to the text, what makes the Gobi a desert?
o: It lies in both Mongolia and China.
It receives very little rain and snow.
It has winter temperatures below −30 °C.
It has extremely hot summer days.
questions.e: The text says what makes the Gobi a desert is low precipitation, not heat. The cold temperatures are a detail about its winters, not the reason it counts as a desert.

questions.s:
When the textile firm in Faisalabad installed solar panels on its factory roofs, managers expected the main gain to be lower electricity bills. The bills did fall, but managers say the bigger change was reliability. Before the panels, power cuts stopped the looms several times a week, and each restart wasted thread and time. With solar power and batteries, the looms now run through most outages.

According to the text, what did managers consider the most important result of installing solar panels?
o: The looms stopped far less often because of power cuts.
The firm used less thread to produce each piece of cloth.
The factory roofs were protected from summer heat.
The firm's electricity bills fell to almost nothing.
questions.e: Managers say 'the bigger change was reliability': looms now run through most outages. Lower bills did happen, but the text ranks them below reliability and never says they fell to almost nothing.

questions.s:
Archaeologists once believed that the people of Mohenjo-daro planned their city's grid of streets and drains all at once. Excavations of the lowest layers now suggest a more gradual story. Early houses were built along paths that already ran roughly north to south, and later builders kept and straightened those lines when they rebuilt. The famous grid, in this view, was less a single design than the result of centuries of careful maintenance.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Mohenjo-daro's street grid may have developed gradually rather than being planned at once.
Mohenjo-daro's early builders ignored the paths that existed before them.
Archaeologists now doubt that Mohenjo-daro ever had a grid of streets.
Mohenjo-daro's drains were added many centuries after its streets were first laid out.
questions.e: The text replaces the idea of a single plan with a grid shaped over centuries as builders kept and straightened older paths. The option doubting the grid existed goes too far: the text still calls it 'the famous grid'.

questions.s:
The red panda spends most of its life in trees in the forests of the eastern Himalayas. Although it belongs to the order of meat-eating mammals, almost all of its diet is bamboo leaves. Because bamboo provides little energy, the red panda sleeps for much of the day and moves slowly to save energy.

Based on the text, why does the red panda sleep for much of the day?
o: Its main food gives it little energy.
It hunts other animals mostly at night.
It is the only mammal in its forest.
It cannot climb trees during daylight.
questions.e: The text links the panda's long sleep to bamboo providing little energy. The option about night hunting is wrong because the text says almost all its diet is bamboo.

questions.s:
Teachers at a Peshawar college tried replacing some lectures with short videos students watched at home, using class time for problem-solving instead. Exam scores rose only slightly. What changed most, the teachers reported, was attendance at office hours: students who had struggled during class problem-solving began seeking help far earlier in the term than students in previous years had.

According to the text, what was the most noticeable effect of the change?
o: Struggling students asked for help much earlier in the term.
Teachers spent less time preparing for their classes.
Students stopped watching lectures and skipped class instead.
Exam scores rose far more than the teachers had expected.
questions.e: The text says what changed most was earlier office-hour visits by struggling students. Exam scores rose only slightly, so the option claiming a large rise contradicts the text.

questions.s:
Critics have often read the Mexican painter Frida Kahlo's self-portraits as private diaries of pain. The art historian Lucía Medina argues that this reading misses how deliberately public the paintings were. Kahlo, Medina notes, chose clothing, jewellery and backgrounds that referred to Mexican history and politics, and she exhibited the works widely. The portraits, on this view, were statements about national identity as much as records of personal suffering.

Which choice best states Medina's main claim?
o: Kahlo's self-portraits were never meant to show any personal suffering.
Kahlo's paintings were rarely exhibited during her lifetime.
Kahlo's clothing in her portraits was chosen mainly for its bright colours.
Kahlo's self-portraits also made public statements about Mexican identity.
questions.e: Medina argues the portraits were 'statements about national identity as much as records of personal suffering', so she adds a public meaning without denying the private one. The option saying they never showed suffering overstates her view.

questions.s:
The Karakoram Highway links Pakistan and China across some of the highest mountains on Earth. Building it took about twenty years, and hundreds of workers lost their lives to rockfalls, landslides and accidents. Today the road carries trade, tourists and supplies to villages that were once cut off for months each winter.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: The Karakoram Highway was very costly to build but now connects remote places.
Rockfalls on the Karakoram Highway have stopped completely.
Tourists now outnumber traders on the Karakoram Highway.
The Karakoram Highway is closed for several months during every single winter.
questions.e: The text pairs the road's human cost with its present role connecting villages once cut off. The winter-closure option twists the detail: villages were cut off before the road, not the road itself.

questions.s:
Ayesha Raza, a marine ecologist, studies mangrove forests along the coast near Karachi. Mangroves are often valued as nurseries for fish, but Raza's measurements highlight another role. The trees' tangled roots trap mud carried by tides, and over time this builds up the shoreline. In places where mangroves were cleared for building, the coast has retreated by several metres in a decade.

Based on the text, what role of mangroves do Raza's measurements highlight?
o: They help build up and hold the shoreline.
They clean pollution from the water around Karachi.
They supply timber that is used in coastal building projects.
They provide breeding places for coastal fish.
questions.e: Raza's work shows roots trapping mud and building the shore, with coasts retreating where mangroves were cleared. The fish-nursery role is the familiar one the text sets aside as 'often valued', not what her measurements highlight.

questions.s:
For years, the town library in a small Punjab district had few visitors after school hours. Then the librarian, Tariq Mehmood, moved the computers from a back room to the main hall and began holding weekly sessions on writing job applications. Within a year, evening visits had tripled. Mehmood says most new visitors came first for the computers but stayed to borrow books.

According to the text, what first attracted most of the new visitors?
o: The job offers that were advertised on the library walls
The new books that the library had bought that year
The quiet reading room that opened in the evenings after school
The computers that had been moved to the main hall
questions.e: Mehmood says most new visitors 'came first for the computers'. Borrowing books came afterwards, and the text never mentions new books being bought.

questions.s:
Linguists have long noted that Urdu and Hindi share most of their grammar and everyday vocabulary. A recent study of radio broadcasts found that the gap between them widens sharply in formal registers. News bulletins in Urdu drew heavily on Persian and Arabic words, while those in Hindi drew on Sanskrit, so that listeners who understood each other's casual conversation sometimes struggled with each other's news.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Radio listeners prefer news bulletins that use mostly casual everyday vocabulary.
Urdu and Hindi are closest in everyday speech and drift apart in formal language.
Hindi has borrowed more words from Persian than Urdu has in recent decades.
Urdu and Hindi have entirely different grammar despite sharing words.
questions.e: The study found shared casual speech but widening differences in formal registers such as news. The grammar option contradicts the opening sentence, which says the languages share most of their grammar.

questions.s:
Most plants open the pores on their leaves during the day to take in carbon dioxide, losing water as they do. Cactuses reverse this pattern. They keep their pores closed through the hot day and open them at night, when the air is cooler and less water evaporates. The carbon dioxide is stored overnight as an acid and used for photosynthesis once the sun rises.

According to the text, why do cactuses open their pores at night?
o: To keep their leaves cool during the hottest hours of the afternoon
To take in carbon dioxide while losing less water
To absorb sunlight more efficiently for photosynthesis
To release the acid that they made during the day
questions.e: Night opening lets cactuses take in carbon dioxide when cooler air means less evaporation. The acid option reverses the process: the acid is made at night to store carbon dioxide, not released then.

questions.s:
In 2010, floods covered about a fifth of Pakistan's land. Afterwards, volunteers in many villages set up early-warning groups. When a river began to rise, members sent messages by phone and loudspeaker so that families could move their animals and belongings to higher ground in time.

According to the text, what was the purpose of the village early-warning groups?
o: To measure how much land the 2010 floods had covered
To give families time to move to safety when rivers rose
To build stronger walls along the banks of every river nearby
To sell phones and loudspeakers to families in villages
questions.e: The groups sent warnings so families could move animals and belongings to higher ground in time. Measuring flood area is a fact the text mentions about 2010, not the groups' task.

questions.s:
The Dutch painter Johannes Vermeer completed fewer than forty known paintings, far fewer than most artists of his time. Some historians blame his slow pace on poor health or family duties. Others point to his materials: Vermeer used costly pigments such as ground lapis lazuli and built up his surfaces in many thin layers, a method that demanded time and money he did not always have.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Historians offer different explanations for why Vermeer produced so few paintings.
Vermeer's paintings were less valued than those of artists who painted more.
Vermeer was the only painter of his time to use lapis lazuli in his work.
Vermeer painted slowly because he refused to use expensive materials.
questions.e: The text sets out two explanations, health and family on one side, costly layered methods on the other. The materials option reverses the text, which says he did use expensive pigments.

questions.s:
Start-ups in Lahore often struggle to hire software engineers, who are drawn to higher salaries abroad. One firm, run by Sana Javed, tried a different tactic. Instead of matching foreign salaries, it offered engineers a four-day week and paid for courses of their choosing. Staff turnover fell by half in two years, though salaries at the firm remained below the market average.

Based on the text, what does Javed's experience suggest?
o: A four-day week raises the output of every software engineer.
Firms in Lahore must pay foreign salaries to keep their staff.
Benefits other than pay can help a firm keep its engineers.
Lahore engineers care more about courses than about salary.
questions.e: Turnover fell by half even though pay stayed below average, suggesting non-salary benefits helped retention. The claim that engineers care more about courses than salary goes beyond one firm's results.

questions.s:
Ice cores drilled from glaciers hold tiny bubbles of ancient air, and scientists use them to reconstruct past climates. A team working in the Himalayas warns that this archive is disappearing. As glaciers warm, meltwater seeps down through the ice and mixes layers that once lay in order, blurring the record before it can be drilled. The team is now racing to collect cores from the most threatened glaciers first.

According to the text, why is the team collecting cores from the most threatened glaciers first?
o: Those glaciers contain the oldest air bubbles anywhere in the Himalayas.
Those glaciers are the easiest to reach with heavy drilling equipment.
Meltwater makes the ice in those glaciers easier to drill through.
Melting is damaging the layered record those glaciers contain.
questions.e: Meltwater mixes layers and blurs the record, so the team takes the most threatened cores first. The text never says those glaciers hold the oldest air, so that option adds an unsupported reason.

questions.s:
Chess was once thought to have been invented in Persia, but most historians now trace it to India around the sixth century. The early Indian game, called chaturanga, had pieces representing infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. Traders later carried it to Persia, where it was renamed and spread further west.

According to the text, where do most historians now believe chess began?
o: In China, as a game played by soldiers on horseback
In Europe, after it spread from Persia westward
In India, as a game called chaturanga
In Persia, before traders carried it east
questions.e: The text says most historians now trace chess to India, where it was called chaturanga. Persia is the older belief the text corrects; it was where the game was later renamed.

questions.s:
When a tea-processing cooperative in Mansehra began selling directly to city shops, its members expected higher prices. Prices rose only a little. The larger gain was information: shopkeepers told the cooperative which blends and package sizes sold fastest, and members changed what they produced. Within three seasons, the cooperative's unsold stock had almost disappeared.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Selling directly greatly raised the prices that the cooperative's members received.
City shopkeepers forced the cooperative to stop producing its own tea blends.
Selling directly gave the cooperative useful knowledge that reduced unsold stock.
The cooperative stopped selling tea after three seasons of losses.
questions.e: The text says prices rose only a little and the bigger gain was information that cut unsold stock. The option about greatly higher prices contradicts 'Prices rose only a little'.

questions.s:
Penguins cannot fly, but their wings are not useless. Over millions of years, penguin wings became stiff, flat flippers. In water, penguins beat these flippers much as other birds beat their wings in air, and some species can swim faster than 30 kilometres per hour.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Penguins lost the ability to fly only a few hundred years ago.
Penguins swim faster than any other bird in the oceans.
Penguin wings have become flippers that are well suited to swimming.
Penguins can fly short distances when they are chased by predators.
questions.e: The text explains how penguin wings became flippers used to 'fly' through water. It gives a speed for some species but never compares penguins with all other birds.

questions.s:
Researchers in Multan compared two groups of cotton farmers. One group received printed leaflets on controlling pests; the other attended field days where trained farmers showed the methods on real crops. A season later, both groups knew the methods equally well when tested, but farmers who attended field days were far more likely to have actually used them on their own land.

According to the text, how did the two groups of farmers differ?
o: Field-day farmers were more likely to put the methods into practice.
Field-day farmers scored much higher on a test of the methods.
Leaflet farmers grew more cotton than field-day farmers did.
Leaflet farmers stopped controlling pests on their land entirely.
questions.e: Both groups knew the methods equally well, but field-day farmers used them more. The option about test scores contradicts the statement that both groups did equally well when tested.

questions.s:
The philosopher Al-Farabi, writing in the tenth century, is often remembered for adapting Greek ideas about the ideal city. Scholar Nadia Hamid argues that his originality lay elsewhere. Al-Farabi, she points out, wrote at length on music theory, measuring intervals and describing instruments with a precision that Greek writers had not attempted. For Hamid, his musical writings, not his political ones, show him at his most inventive.

Which choice best states Hamid's claim about Al-Farabi?
o: His writing on music was more original than his political philosophy.
His political ideas were copied word for word from earlier Greek writers.
His musical writings were unknown until scholars rediscovered them.
He was the first scholar to invent the musical instruments he described.
questions.e: Hamid says his originality 'lay elsewhere' and that his musical writings show him 'most inventive'. The word-for-word option overstates 'adapting'; Hamid does not call the political work copied.

questions.s:
Food waste is usually blamed on households, but a study of Pakistan's mango trade found large losses much earlier. Up to a third of the fruit was spoiled before it reached markets, mostly because it was packed in heavy stacks without cooling and bruised during long truck journeys. Simple changes, such as shallow crates and travel at night, cut these losses sharply in trials.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Expensive refrigerated trucks are the only way to prevent mangoes from spoiling.
Most mango waste in Pakistan is caused by households throwing away fruit.
Mangoes in Pakistan should only be sold in markets close to the farms.
Much mango waste happens during transport and can be reduced with simple changes.
questions.e: The study locates losses in packing and transport and shows that shallow crates and night travel help. The refrigerated-truck option contradicts the point that 'simple changes' cut losses.

questions.s:
The Badshahi Mosque in Lahore was completed in 1673 under the emperor Aurangzeb. Its courtyard can hold tens of thousands of worshippers. For more than three centuries it was one of the largest mosques in the world, and it remains one of Lahore's best-known landmarks.

According to the text, when was the Badshahi Mosque completed?
o: In 1673, before Aurangzeb's reign
In 1673, during Aurangzeb's reign
Three centuries after Aurangzeb's death
In the reign of the emperor Akbar
questions.e: The text says the mosque was completed in 1673 under Aurangzeb. The option placing it before his reign keeps the right year but contradicts 'under the emperor Aurangzeb'.

questions.s:
Sleep scientists have found that teenagers' body clocks shift later during puberty, so that many cannot fall asleep before about 11 p.m. When a group of schools in one country moved their start time from 7:30 to 8:30 a.m., students slept on average forty minutes longer, and fewer were late or absent. Teachers also reported fewer students dozing in morning lessons.

Based on the text, why did later school start times help students?
o: They gave teachers more time to prepare their morning lessons.
They better matched teenagers' naturally later sleep patterns.
They made teenagers go to bed earlier than they used to before.
They shortened the school day so that students were less tired.
questions.e: Because teenagers' clocks shift later, a later start let them sleep forty minutes more. The option about going to bed earlier is wrong; the text explains that many cannot fall asleep before 11 p.m.

questions.s:
In many accounts, the printing press spread literacy by making books cheap. Historian Imran Qureshi argues that in parts of South Asia the order was reversed. There, he notes, networks of scribes, schools and lending libraries had already created large reading publics before printing arrived in the nineteenth century, and it was the existence of these readers that made printing presses profitable enough to establish.

Which choice best states Qureshi's argument?
o: Printing presses spread literacy across South Asia by making books cheap.
Lending libraries in South Asia closed soon after printing presses arrived.
Scribes in South Asia opposed printing presses because they feared losing work.
In parts of South Asia, readers came first and helped printing take hold.
questions.e: Qureshi reverses the usual story: existing reading publics made printing profitable. The option about printing spreading literacy is exactly the account he says does not fit parts of South Asia.

questions.s:
Some spiders spin a new web every day. At dawn or dusk, the spider eats the old silk, which is rich in protein, and then uses that protein to make fresh threads. In this way it saves much of the energy it would otherwise need to produce new silk.

According to the text, why do some spiders eat their old webs?
o: To catch insects that are stuck in the old silk
To hide their webs from birds during the night
To make their new webs larger than the old ones
To reuse the protein in the silk for new threads
questions.e: The spider eats the protein-rich silk and reuses it to make new threads, saving energy. Eating trapped insects is a plausible guess, but the text gives recycling protein as the reason.

questions.s:
Hockey was long Pakistan's most successful sport, with Olympic gold medals in 1960, 1968 and 1984. Former players interviewed for a recent documentary agree that the national team declined after the 1990s, but they disagree about why. Some blame the switch to artificial turf, which was rare in Pakistan; others point to falling investment in school and club hockey.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Former players agree that Pakistani hockey declined but differ on the causes.
Former players believe Pakistani hockey has improved since the 1990s.
Artificial turf was the only cause of the decline of Pakistani hockey.
Pakistan won more Olympic gold medals in hockey than any other nation.
questions.e: The players agree on the decline but 'disagree about why', naming turf and falling investment. Calling turf the only cause ignores the second explanation.

questions.s:
Camels can go for days without drinking, but not because they store water in their humps. The humps hold fat. Camels survive dry spells because their bodies lose very little water: their kidneys produce concentrated urine and their body temperature can rise during the day without making them sweat.

According to the text, what is stored in a camel's hump?
o: Fat
Urine
Water
Sweat
questions.e: The text says plainly that 'The humps hold fat.' Water is the popular belief the text corrects.

questions.s:
Bilal started a small repair stall for mobile phones in Rawalpindi. At first he fixed only cracked screens. When customers kept asking about batteries and charging ports, he taught himself those repairs from online videos. Within a year, screen repairs made up less than half of his work.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Bilal widened his repair work in response to what customers asked for.
Bilal learned phone repair at a technical college in Rawalpindi.
Bilal's customers mostly needed new phones rather than repairs.
Bilal stopped repairing cracked screens because the work did not pay enough.
questions.e: Customer requests led Bilal to learn battery and port repairs, so screens became under half his work. He did not stop screen repairs; they simply became a smaller share.

questions.s:
Many people assume that a forest absorbs more carbon the older it gets. Studies of tropical forests suggest otherwise. Young, fast-growing forests on cleared land often take up carbon more quickly than old forests, whose growth has slowed. Old forests, however, hold far more carbon in total, stored in their massive trunks and deep soils.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Old forests absorb carbon faster than any young forest can manage to.
Young forests should replace old forests to reduce carbon in the air.
Young forests absorb carbon faster, but old forests store much more of it.
Forests stop storing carbon once they reach a certain age.
questions.e: The text contrasts the rate of uptake (faster in young forests) with total storage (greater in old ones). The replacement option draws a policy conclusion the text never makes and ignores the stored carbon in old forests.

questions.s:
The Urdu writer Saadat Hasan Manto was put on trial several times for stories that officials called obscene. Manto replied that his stories were not obscene; society was. He argued that a writer who described cruelty and hypocrisy honestly should not be blamed for what he saw. Many readers today regard those same stories as his finest work.

According to the text, how did Manto respond to the charge that his stories were obscene?
o: He said the officials had not read his stories carefully enough.
He said his stories honestly reflected faults that existed in society.
He agreed and promised to write gentler stories in the future.
He argued that writers should be free to invent cruel events for entertainment.
questions.e: Manto said society, not his stories, was obscene and that he described cruelty honestly. The 'invent for entertainment' option misreads him: he claimed to report what he saw, not to invent it.

questions.s:
Electric cars produce no exhaust while driving, but their overall effect on air quality depends on where their electricity comes from. A study of several countries found that where power stations burned mostly coal, electric cars cut city air pollution but added to pollution near the power stations. Where electricity came mainly from hydropower or solar, the benefit was clear everywhere.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Electric cars have no effect at all on air quality in any country.
How clean electric cars are depends largely on how their electricity is produced.
Coal power stations are mostly built inside crowded cities in many countries.
Electric cars produce more exhaust while driving than petrol cars produce.
questions.e: The study shows the benefit is clear with hydro or solar power but mixed with coal. The exhaust option contradicts the first sentence, which says electric cars produce no exhaust while driving.

questions.s:
Historians of Lahore's Anarkali Bazaar usually trace its prosperity to its location near the old city. Shopkeepers' account books from the 1920s suggest that this is only part of the story. They show that many traders extended credit to regular customers for months at a time, and that these long-term ties, more than passing trade, kept the bazaar busy during years when the city's economy slowed.

Based on the text, what do the account books suggest about Anarkali Bazaar?
o: Its busiest years were those in which the city's economy slowed down.
Its location near the old city did nothing at all to help its trade.
Its traders refused to sell on credit because of earlier losses.
Long-term credit ties with customers helped it survive slow economic years.
questions.e: The books show traders giving months of credit, ties that 'kept the bazaar busy' in slow years. The location option overstates the text, which calls location 'only part of the story', not irrelevant.

questions.s:
A rainbow appears when sunlight passes into raindrops, bends, reflects off the back of each drop and bends again as it leaves. Because each colour of light bends by a slightly different amount, the colours separate into bands. That is why a rainbow can be seen only when the sun is behind the viewer.

According to the text, why do the colours of a rainbow separate into bands?
o: The viewer's eyes split white light into separate colours.
Each raindrop holds only one colour of light at a time.
The sun gives out each colour at a different time of day.
Each colour of light bends by a slightly different amount.
questions.e: The text explains that different colours bend by different amounts, separating them. Nothing suggests a drop holds only one colour.

questions.s:
In a Quetta hospital, nurses noticed that patients often missed doses of medicine after going home. Rather than giving longer instructions, the nurses began handing out simple charts with pictures of the sun and moon to show morning and evening doses. Follow-up calls a month later found that patients using the charts missed far fewer doses than before.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
o: Longer written instructions helped patients remember their doses better.
Nurses in Quetta began making follow-up calls instead of giving charts.
Simple picture charts helped patients take their medicine more reliably at home.
Patients in Quetta preferred evening doses to morning doses of medicine.
questions.e: The nurses replaced longer instructions with picture charts, and missed doses fell. The option praising longer instructions reverses what the nurses chose.

questions.s:
The Silk Road is often imagined as a single route along which caravans travelled from China to Europe. Historians now describe it as a web of shorter routes. Most traders covered only one stretch, selling goods to the next group of merchants, so that silk might change hands many times before reaching the Mediterranean.

According to the text, how did most Silk Road traders operate?
o: They avoided selling goods to other merchants along the route.
They travelled only by sea instead of crossing the land routes.
They carried silk all the way from China to the Mediterranean themselves.
They travelled only part of the way and passed goods on to others.
questions.e: The text says most traders covered one stretch and sold goods to the next merchants. The option about carrying silk all the way is the popular image the text corrects.

questions.s:
Some psychologists claimed that people make worse decisions when given too many choices. Later attempts to repeat the original experiments produced mixed results: in some studies, large menus discouraged buyers, while in others they made no difference. A review of these studies concluded that too much choice is harmful mainly when options are hard to compare and people are unsure what they want.

Based on the text, what did the review conclude about having many choices?
o: Many choices always lead people to make worse decisions.
Many choices cause problems mainly under particular conditions.
Many choices help people most when they are unsure of what they want.
Many choices never affect the decisions that people make.
questions.e: The review found harm 'mainly when options are hard to compare and people are unsure', so the effect depends on conditions. 'Always' and 'never' both ignore the mixed results.

questions.s:
Rohtas Fort, near Jhelum, was built in the sixteenth century by Sher Shah Suri. Its walls stretch for about four kilometres and include twelve gates. The fort was designed to control the road between Peshawar and Lahore and to block rebels in the hills nearby.

According to the text, what was one purpose of Rohtas Fort?
o: To serve as Sher Shah Suri's main royal palace
To protect traders who crossed the river by boat
To store grain for the city of Jhelum in winter
To control the road between Peshawar and Lahore
questions.e: The text states the fort was designed to control the Peshawar-Lahore road and block rebels. The palace and grain options are not mentioned.

questions.s:
Fatima's chemistry class tested whether salt dissolves faster in hot or cold water. Every group found that it dissolved faster in hot water. But when Fatima's group repeated the test without stirring, the difference between hot and cold water became much larger, leading the class to realise that stirring had been hiding part of the temperature effect.

Based on the text, what did Fatima's group discover?
o: Salt dissolved faster in cold water when the mixture was not stirred.
Salt dissolved at the same rate in hot and cold water once stirring stopped.
Stirring had no effect on how quickly salt dissolved in either sample.
Stirring had reduced the measured difference between hot and cold water.
questions.e: Without stirring the hot-cold gap grew much larger, showing stirring had been masking part of the temperature effect. The option saying stirring had no effect contradicts the changed results.

questions.s:
