• Some routes passed through what is now northern Pakistan.

The student wants to emphasize that the Silk Road carried more than goods. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes that linked China with the Mediterranean world.
Merchants on the Silk Road traded goods such as silk, spices, paper and glass.
Some of the Silk Road's routes passed through what is now northern Pakistan.
Besides silk and spices, the Silk Road carried ideas and religions, among them Buddhism.
questions.e: Only this choice mentions the ideas and religions that travelled along with trade goods. The choice about silk, spices, paper and glass lists only goods, which is the opposite of the goal.

questions.s:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Scientists measure air pollution using tiny particles called PM2.5.
• The World Health Organization recommends a yearly PM2.5 average of no more than 5 micrograms per cubic metre.
• A 2023 study measured a yearly average of 85 micrograms per cubic metre in an industrial city.
• A nearby hill town measured 22 micrograms per cubic metre.

The student wants to emphasize how far both places exceeded the WHO guideline. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
o: A 2023 study found a yearly PM2.5 average of 85 micrograms per cubic metre in an industrial city.
Both places exceeded the WHO guideline of 5 micrograms: the hill town by more than four times, the industrial city by seventeen times.
The WHO recommends that yearly PM2.5 levels average no more than 5 micrograms per cubic metre.
The industrial city's yearly average of 85 micrograms was nearly four times the hill town's 22 micrograms.
questions.e: Comparing each place with the guideline gives 22 ÷ 5 = 4.4 and 85 ÷ 5 = 17, as this choice states. The choice comparing 85 with 22 is accurate but compares the two places with each other, not with the WHO guideline.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The grey mangrove is the only tree able to survive in the salty, oxygen-poor creeks to the south of Karachi.
Replanting projects along the coast have now fully reversed the damage done to the delta by upstream irrigation.
Of all the mangrove's adaptations, its pneumatophores matter most, because they let the tree breathe at low tide.
The grey mangrove copes with salt and poor mud through costly adaptations, and reduced river flow is straining them.
questions.e: The passage explains how the tree handles salt and low oxygen, then shows that these adaptations cost energy and are strained as less river water reaches the delta. It calls Avicennia the hardiest of the local species, so other species exist, and it says replanting has restored large areas, not that the damage is reversed.

questions.s: According to the passage, what happens to the salt that gets past the mangrove's roots?
o: It is stored in older leaves, which the tree then sheds.
The pneumatophores release it into the air at low tide.
Glands in the leaves push it out onto the leaf surface.
The root membranes return it to the creek on each tide.
questions.e: The second paragraph says the salt that slips through is carried to the leaves, where glands pump it onto the surface as crystals. The pneumatophores are described only as channels for air, not salt.

questions.s: Based on the passage, a grey mangrove in a creek where river water still dilutes the seawater would most likely
o: grow better, since less of its energy would go into removing salt.
lose its pneumatophores, since it would no longer need them at all.
stop forming salt crystals on its leaves at any time of the year.
be crowded out quickly by less hardy kinds of mangrove in the area.
questions.e: The third paragraph links salt-pumping to lost growth and says the river's flood once kept that cost manageable, so less salt means more energy for growth. The pneumatophores deal with oxygen, which dilution does not change, and diluted seawater is still salty, so crystals would not stop altogether.

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage mainly serves to
o: separate the trees' ability to endure from the health of the forest as a whole.
contradict the earlier statement that replanting projects have been successful.
suggest that Avicennia should be replaced with mangrove species that grow faster.
summarise the particular adaptations that were described in the second paragraph.
questions.e: After granting that the mangroves are not doomed, the author warns that survival is not the same as health, distinguishing individual toughness from a thriving forest. The sentence does not deny the replanting success mentioned just before; it qualifies what that toughness proves.

questions.s: The main purpose of the passage is to
o: explain a kind of friction, using the bowed violin string as its main example.
argue that the violin is harder to learn than any other string instrument.
describe how Helmholtz designed and built a new kind of vibrating microscope.
propose several practical ways for engineers to make car brakes quieter.
questions.e: The passage defines stick-slip motion, walks through it in detail with the bow, and closes with other examples of the same effect. Brakes and the difficulty of learning appear only as supporting details, and the passage says Helmholtz used the microscope, not that he built it.

questions.s: According to the passage, the rosin on a bow's hair
o: lowers the tension in the string so that the string can vibrate more freely.
widens the gap between the force that starts sliding and the force that keeps it going.
protects the hair from wearing out after many hours of regular playing.
stops the string from ever slipping past the hair while the bow moves.
questions.e: The second paragraph says rosin makes the difference between the starting and sliding forces unusually large. It does not stop slipping altogether; the string breaks free in every cycle, which is how the note is made.

questions.s: Based on the passage, which change would most likely make a squealing door hinge quieter?
o: Making the friction that starts motion closer to the friction during motion
Coating the hinge with a sticky resin like rosin to increase its grip
Making the door heavier so that it swings open more slowly each time
Opening the door faster so that each stick-slip cycle is shorter
questions.e: The last paragraph says designers fight squeals by making the two kinds of friction nearly equal, since stick-slip depends on the gap between them. A rosin-like coating would widen that gap and make the squeal worse.

questions.s: The passage presents Helmholtz's observation mainly as
o: evidence that a bowed string moves in the smooth curve that players must control.
a finding that corrected an earlier assumption and showed why technique matters.
a historical curiosity with little bearing on how players are taught today.
proof that the rosin on a bow wears away at a steady rate during each note.
questions.e: Helmholtz found a sharp corner rather than the smooth curve people had assumed, and the passage says his work helped explain why bowing pressure matters. The smooth curve is the assumption he overturned, so the option built on it reverses the passage.

questions.s: Which choice best summarises the passage?
o: Mehrgarh matters mainly because it shows where farming first began anywhere in the world.
The bead-makers of Mehrgarh traded their flint drills with communities across South Asia.
Researchers have proved that the people of Mehrgarh drilled teeth in order to treat decay.
Drilled molars from Mehrgarh point to an early form of dentistry that later disappeared.
questions.e: Most of the passage describes the drilled teeth, the evidence that they were treated in living people, and the puzzle of why the practice ended. The researchers explicitly say the purpose could not be proved, so the claim that they proved it overstates the evidence.

questions.s: According to the passage, the researchers ruled out decoration as the reason for the holes because the holes
o: contained traces of a filling material.
showed circular grooves from a drill.
were found only in bead-makers' graves.
were on teeth at the back of the mouth.
questions.e: The third paragraph says the holes were at the back of the mouth, where they could not have served as decoration. The grooves are real evidence, but they show that a rotating tool was used, not that the holes were not ornamental.

questions.s: The passage indicates that the smoothing of some holes' edges by chewing shows that
o: the drilling must have been carried out after the person had died.
at least some people lived on and used the tooth after it was drilled.
the people of Mehrgarh ate an unusually coarse and gritty diet.
the holes were first made by decay and only later by a tool.
questions.e: Chewing could smooth the edges only if the person kept eating after the work was done, so some patients survived the procedure. That same reasoning rules out drilling after death.

questions.s: In the final paragraph, the author's attitude toward explanations for the end of the practice is best described as
o: confident that it ended because it failed to relieve any pain.
dismissive of the idea that the tools of Mehrgarh ever changed.
critical of researchers for neglecting the settlement's later graves.
tentative, since the evidence cannot decide between possibilities.
questions.e: The author offers two possibilities with "Perhaps" and then states that the evidence cannot settle the matter. The pain explanation is only one of the options raised, not a conclusion the author commits to.

questions.s: Which choice best states the central claim of the passage?
o: Standard time spread because railways needed coordination, not because local time was inaccurate.
Local solar time was a superstition that science gradually replaced during the nineteenth century.
North American railways adopted standard time earlier and more smoothly than British ones did.
The telegraph, more than the railway, was the main reason towns gave up keeping their own time.
questions.e: The final paragraph states the claim directly: local time was accurate, and the railways made a more useful time, not a truer one. The author names the science-over-superstition story only to reject it.

questions.s: According to the passage, what happened in Britain in 1880?
o: A railway first ran its trains on London time.
Greenwich time became the legal standard.
A conference chose the Greenwich meridian.
The telegraph first carried a time signal.
questions.e: The second paragraph says Parliament made Greenwich time the legal standard in 1880. The Great Western Railway's switch came in 1840, and the meridian conference was held in Washington in 1884.

questions.s: The passage suggests that some public clocks had two minute hands mainly because
o: the law required every town in Britain to display London time from 1840.
clockmakers of the period could not keep a single minute hand accurate.
travellers wished to compare British time with the time in North America.
local time and railway time were both in use while towns made the change.
questions.e: The clocks showed both the railway's time and local time, which makes sense only while the two were in use side by side during the transition. The legal standard came in 1880, so no law forced towns to show London time in 1840.

questions.s: The author mentions "a victory of science over superstition" in order to
o: support the view that local solar time rested on mistaken popular beliefs.
show that scientists opposed the railways' choice of a single standard time.
explain why a number of towns resisted railway time for so many years.
introduce a reading of the history that the author then goes on to reject.
questions.e: The phrase is followed at once by "That account misses the point" and by the claim that local solar time was not wrong. The author raises the view in order to dismiss it, so it cannot be support for that view.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Rereading is a useless way to study, and students should replace it entirely with tests that are graded.
Recalling material from memory builds longer-lasting learning than rereading, though it feels less effective.
Students learn best when every lesson ends with a short written examination that the teacher marks.
Rereading gives better results than practising recall when students are tested just a few minutes after study.
questions.e: The passage argues that retrieval practice produces more durable learning even though learners judge it less effective. Rereading does win on an immediate test, but that is one detail of the experiment, and the author says the benefit lasts a week, not five minutes.

questions.s: According to the passage, in the typical experiment the group that practised recalling
o: did better than the rereaders on both the early and the later test.
read the passage four times in all before it was finally tested.
did slightly worse after five minutes but better a week later.
was graded on its recall, which made its members work harder.
questions.e: The second paragraph says the rereaders usually do slightly better after five minutes and that the pattern reverses after a week. The author stresses that the benefit does not come from being graded.

questions.s: The survey results described in the fourth paragraph suggest that learners
o: come to prefer retrieval practice once they see their improved scores.
remember more when they are free to choose their own way of studying.
may not be reliable judges of which study methods help them most.
find rereading uncomfortable because it exposes the gaps in what they know.
questions.e: Learners rated retrieval as less effective even after their own scores showed it worked better, so their sense of what helps is unreliable. That same finding rules out the idea that they switch preference once they see the scores.

questions.s: As used in the final paragraph, "proportion" most nearly means
o: balance
symmetry
dimension
fairness
questions.e: The author has just granted that rereading has a place, so "proportion" refers to the balance between rereading and recall in a student's time. Symmetry and dimension describe shape or size, which do not fit a point about how study time is shared.

questions.s: The passage is mainly concerned with
o: comparing Islamabad with older capital cities that grew without any plan.
arguing that informal settlements should be cleared from Islamabad's edges.
explaining why the Margalla Hills were chosen as the site of the capital.
describing the ideas behind Islamabad's plan and where they fell short.
questions.e: The passage sets out Doxiadis's dynapolis and sector ideas, notes what worked, and ends with the plan's blind spot. Older unplanned capitals appear only in the opening contrast, and the author describes informal settlements without recommending their removal.

questions.s: According to the passage, the broad avenues between sectors were meant to
o: mark the outer limits of each sector's central market and its shops.
allow the centre of the city to move forward as the city grew larger.
carry through traffic so that streets inside the sectors stayed quiet.
provide green spaces within easy walking distance of every household.
questions.e: The third paragraph says through traffic would stay on the avenues, leaving the interior streets quiet. A moving centre is the purpose of the dynapolis as a whole, not of the avenues.

questions.s: Based on the passage, Doxiadis would most likely have criticised a city in which
o: each neighbourhood has its own market that residents can reach on foot.
homes are identified by letters and numbers that follow a regular grid pattern.
growth takes place mainly in one direction along a band that keeps widening.
all new suburbs depend on roads that lead to one fixed central district.
questions.e: Doxiadis argued that a city growing in rings from one core chokes its centre because every new suburb sends traffic to the same streets. Growth in one direction along a widening band is his own dynapolis, so he would have approved of it.

questions.s: In the final sentence, "the city that actually arrived" refers to
o: the people and settlements that the plan made no provision for.
the visitors who still admire Islamabad's greenery and addresses.
the sectors that were completed exactly as the master plan required.
the government offices that moved to the foot of the Margalla Hills.
questions.e: The sentence contrasts the planned city with the residents who could not afford the sectors and settled informally, which the grid had no place for. The visitors are mentioned earlier as evidence that parts of the plan succeeded.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The tanpura is the hardest instrument in Hindustani music to master and takes many years of training.
Electronic drones have now replaced the tanpura in most concerts of Hindustani classical music.
Although it plays no melody, the tanpura gives the music its pitch frame and a distinctive sound.
A raga is defined by a fixed scale, which the tanpura plays through before the singer begins.
questions.e: The passage explains how the drone sets the frame for judging pitch and how the bridge creates its shimmer. It says the player sits almost motionless plucking open strings, and that a raga is defined less by a fixed scale than by each note's relation to the tonic.

questions.s: According to the passage, the cotton thread under each string is used to
o: set precisely where the string grazes the curved bridge.
stop the string from touching the bridge as it vibrates.
tune the string to the tonic or to the fifth of the raga.
keep the string from being pressed against the long neck.
questions.e: The third paragraph says the thread adjusts exactly where the string grazes the bridge. The jawari effect depends on the string brushing against the bridge, so stopping that contact would remove the shimmer.

questions.s: It can most reasonably be inferred from the second paragraph that a singer performing without any drone would be
o: unable to perform a raga, because a raga is defined by a drone.
more likely to choose a raga that is built on a simple fixed scale.
less likely to notice when her notes drift slightly off pitch.
obliged to pluck the tonic herself on a second stringed instrument.
questions.e: The paragraph says small drifts in pitch can pass unnoticed without the tanpura but become obvious with it. A raga is defined by each note's relation to the tonic, not by the drone itself, so the singer could still perform, only with less control.

questions.s: The final paragraph mainly serves to
o: note a modern substitute and give performers' reason for still preferring the original.
argue that students who practise with apps can never become skilled concert performers.
describe how instrument makers protect their methods for adjusting the bridge.
show that the tanpura's sound changes from cycle to cycle because it is poorly made.
questions.e: The paragraph mentions drone boxes and apps, then reports that many performers prefer the real tanpura because its slight variation sounds alive. It says many students practise with apps without judging their future skill, and it treats the variation as a strength, not a defect.

questions.s: Which choice best states the central claim of the passage?
o: The case of Vulcan shows that Newton's laws were never as reliable as nineteenth-century scientists believed.
A failed prediction does not show which assumption is at fault, so the right response is often clear only later.
Scientists should always reject a theory as soon as observation contradicts one of its predictions.
Discoveries such as that of Neptune usually owe more to good luck than to careful calculation.
questions.e: The third and fourth paragraphs draw the lesson from the paired stories: a contradicted prediction signals an error somewhere but not where, and the difference between wise defence and stubbornness often appears only in hindsight. The passage questions, rather than recommends, rejecting a theory at the first failed test.

questions.s: According to the passage, astronomers looked for Vulcan especially during solar eclipses because
o: the sun's glare was blocked at those times.
Mercury was closest to the sun at those times.
Le Verrier had said an eclipse would reveal it.
Einstein's theory said it would be visible then.
questions.e: The second paragraph says the searches were made particularly during eclipses, when the sun's glare is blocked. Einstein's theory removed the need for Vulcan altogether, so it predicted no such sighting.

questions.s: The passage suggests that the reported sightings of Vulcan were
o: what persuaded Einstein to develop his new theory of gravity in 1915.
eventually confirmed by astronomers working at the Berlin Observatory.
evidence that Neptune itself had been found by chance, not calculation.
mistaken, since no extra planet was needed to explain Mercury's orbit.
questions.e: None of the sightings was confirmed, and general relativity explained Mercury's motion with no extra planet, so the reports must have been errors. The passage gives no link between the sightings and Einstein's work.

questions.s: The statement "At the time, nobody could have known which was which" primarily serves to
o: criticise Le Verrier for proposing Vulcan without enough supporting evidence.
suggest that Einstein's theory was accepted before it had been properly tested.
stress that the evidence then available could not show which response was right.
imply that the astronomers in Berlin were less skilled than Le Verrier was.
questions.e: The sentence follows the observation that adding an unseen planet was right for Uranus and wrong for Mercury, and it makes the point that this could not be told in advance. Because the author says no one could have known, the sentence excuses Le Verrier rather than criticising him.

questions.s: The passage mainly
o: argues that banks should copy the committee system to attract more customers.
compares Pakistani committees in detail with the tanda of Mexico.
explains why people join committees even though committees pay no interest.
warns that committees usually collapse and should be avoided by savers.
questions.e: The passage poses the puzzle of an arrangement that pays no interest and answers it with timing and commitment. It does mention the risk of collapse, but only where trust is weak, not as a general warning against committees.

questions.s: According to the passage, a committee works like an interest-free loan for most members because they
o: are allowed to repay the pot more slowly than the others.
receive the full pot before they have paid in that much.
get a small extra sum from the organiser every month.
can draw on the pot whenever an emergency comes up.
questions.e: Every member except the last collects Rs 100,000 before contributing that amount, then pays it back in monthly instalments. The passage mentions no extra payments from the organiser, and each member pays the same Rs 10,000 a month.

questions.s: Based on the passage, the member who receives the pot last benefits mainly because
o: she is paid a larger sum than the members whose turns came earlier.
owing payments to neighbours makes a saving plan easier to keep.
she is free to choose the month in which she will collect the pot.
she earns interest from the members who took the pot before her.
questions.e: The third paragraph says even the last member gains, because a monthly payment owed to neighbours is far harder to skip than money kept at home. The passage states that every member receives exactly what she puts in, so the last member gets no larger sum or interest.

questions.s: The sentence "The system's strength, however, is also its risk" suggests that
o: the trust that makes committees work also leaves them open to failure.
committees are strong only when organisers charge a fee for joining.
paying no interest is both an advantage and a drawback of committees.
committees grow riskier as the size of each monthly payment rises.
questions.e: The sentence opens a paragraph explaining that committees rest on trust and social pressure, which nothing else enforces, so a member can disappear with the pot. The lack of interest is discussed earlier and is not what this paragraph calls a risk.

questions.s: Which choice best describes what happens in the passage?
o: A girl's uncle repairs an old radio while she writes a school report on how radios work.
A family argues over whether to sell a valuable radio that has been in storage for years.
A girl repairs her late grandfather's radio and finds the work means more than a school task.
A physics teacher shows his class how valve radios pick up stations from distant cities.
questions.e: Sana takes the radio apart for an assignment, spends the winter repairing it, and is moved when it plays and her grandmother remembers him. Her uncle only advises her on which parts might fail; she does the repair herself.

questions.s: According to the passage, Sana obtained the replacement valves from
o: her uncle, who still kept stock from the electrical goods he sold.
a shopkeeper who found them in a box he had not opened in years.
her teacher, who lent them from the school's physics laboratory.
another old radio that had been stored among the family's trunks.
questions.e: The third paragraph says a shopkeeper in the bazaar found two valves in a long-unopened box. The uncle's role was to tell her which parts were likely to fail.

questions.s: The grandmother's words in the fifth paragraph most strongly suggest that
o: she disapproves of the way Sana is handling such a fragile radio.
Sana's way of tuning the radio reminds her of her late husband.
she had often asked her husband to tune the radio more quickly.
she is surprised that the old radio can still receive any stations.
questions.e: She says he used to turn the dial "exactly like that", so watching Sana brings back her memory of him; her silence all winter and putting down her tea show she is moved. Her affectionate image of the station that "might run away" does not express disapproval or impatience.

questions.s: The final paragraph mainly suggests that Sana
o: regrets that her report for the teacher contained a number of mistakes.
feels her technical report cannot capture what the repair has meant to her.
plans to write a second report about the history of the family radio.
now believes that physics matters less than her family's memories do.
questions.e: Her report is described as entirely correct, yet she thinks none of it was "about this", meaning the experience in the courtyard. The paragraph contrasts two kinds of meaning without ranking physics below family memories.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Lichens are a kind of moss that grows mainly on old stones, rooftops and the bark of roadside trees.
The decline of coal burning has made the air in most industrial cities completely clean again.
The partnership that makes up a lichen leaves it sensitive to polluted air and useful for tracking it.
Lichens grow faster than flowering plants because they take in water directly from rain and mist.
questions.e: The passage moves from the lichen's structure to its sensitivity to sulphur dioxide and its use as a living record of air quality. It says lichens grow only a few millimetres a year, and it warns that their return is not proof of clean air.

questions.s: According to the passage, the fungus in a lichen
o: uses sunlight to make the sugars on which both of the partners depend.
filters sulphur dioxide out of rain before its partner can absorb it.
supplies roots that draw minerals up from the soil beneath the lichen.
forms the body that holds water and attaches the lichen to a surface.
questions.e: The first paragraph says the fungus provides the structure that holds water and anchors the lichen. Making sugars from sunlight is the job of the alga or cyanobacterium, and the second paragraph says lichens have no roots.

questions.s: Based on the passage, a lichen survey can show something that a single instrument reading cannot because
o: lichens respond equally strongly to every kind of air pollutant.
instruments are unable to detect sulphur dioxide in city air.
lichens grow only where the air has always been perfectly clean.
slow-growing lichens reflect a district's conditions over many years.
questions.e: Lichens recover slowly from damage, so the species present record the air over a long period, whereas a reading captures one moment. The final paragraph says lichens respond more strongly to some pollutants than to others, which rules out equal sensitivity.

questions.s: The statement that the return of lichens "is not proof that the air is clean" serves mainly to
o: reject the earlier claim that lichens are harmed by sulphur dioxide in the air.
suggest that coal burning has in fact increased in the cities mentioned.
qualify a hopeful observation by noting a limit of what lichens can show.
argue that instruments should replace lichen surveys in all future studies.
questions.e: Right after reporting the hopeful return of lichens, the author adds a caution: because lichens react more to some pollutants than to others, their return shows only part of the picture. The caution limits the observation; it does not withdraw the earlier point about sulphur dioxide.

questions.s: The main purpose of the passage is to
o: describe skating techniques that reduce the risk of falling on ice.
argue that glass is more slippery than ice at low temperatures.
weigh several explanations for why ice is slippery.
explain how Faraday measured the thickness of the layer on ice.
questions.e: The passage examines pressure melting, frictional heating and Faraday's surface layer in turn and judges how well each works. Skating appears only as an example, and the passage credits modern experiments, not Faraday, with detecting the layer.

questions.s: According to the passage, pressure melting cannot fully explain slippery ice because
o: people slip on ice that is too cold for pressure alone to melt.
skate blades are too wide to concentrate a skater's weight.
squeezing ice raises its melting point rather than lowering it.
frictional heating cools the ice as a skater moves across it.
questions.e: The second paragraph says a blade lowers the melting point by only about a degree, while people slip on ice far colder than that. The passage states that squeezing lowers the melting point, so the claim that it raises it reverses the text.

questions.s: Based on the passage, frictional heating is least able to explain
o: why a skater keeps gliding once she is already moving.
why a person standing still on ice may start to slide.
why a thin film of water can form under a moving blade.
why a sliding shoe warms the ice directly beneath it.
questions.e: Frictional heating needs movement, so it can account for continued sliding but not for the first slip of someone standing still, as the third paragraph notes. Continued gliding is exactly the case it does explain.

questions.s: The final sentence suggests that the pressure-melting explanation lasted so long mainly because
o: Faraday's rival idea was disproved by later experiments.
it was supported by the computer simulations described.
few people tested whether its numbers actually worked.
skaters found that it matched their own experience.
questions.e: The sentence says a familiar explanation can survive "simply because no one checks the arithmetic", echoing the earlier point that the numbers for pressure melting do not add up. The simulations support Faraday's layer, not pressure melting.

questions.s: Which choice best summarises the passage?
o: Tree-ring dating has now replaced radiocarbon dating in nearly every kind of archaeological work.
Trees in tropical forests form the clearest annual rings and are the most useful ones for dating.
Matching ring patterns lets researchers date wood to the year, though the method has clear limits.
A single tree's rings are enough to reveal the weather history of the region in which it grew.
questions.e: The passage explains how overlapping ring patterns are linked, praises the method's precision and then sets out its limits. It compares the method with radiocarbon dating but never says one has replaced the other, and it says tropical trees often lack distinct rings.

questions.s: According to the passage, researchers extend a tree-ring chronology further back by
o: counting the rings of the oldest living tree that they can locate.
joining older timbers whose inner rings overlap with younger samples.
checking the age of each timber with radiocarbon dating first.
comparing ring widths with written records of past droughts.
questions.e: The second paragraph describes matching the inner rings of older timbers to the outer rings of living trees and joining the sequences step by step. Counting the rings of one living tree only gives that tree's age.

questions.s: Based on the passage, which situation would most likely lead to a building being dated too early?
o: Its beams were taken from an older structure that had been pulled down.
Its beams were all cut from trees that were felled in the same winter.
Its beams still have the outermost ring that grew just beneath the bark.
Its beams come from a region with a long and well-established chronology.
questions.e: The method dates the year a tree died, so reused timber from an older building makes a structure look older than it is. A surviving outer ring makes the date more precise, not less reliable.

questions.s: As used in the final sentence, "remembers" most nearly means
o: records
imagines
repeats
celebrates
questions.e: The rings preserve an exact account of the tree's own growth, so "remembers" here means records. "Repeats" would imply the tree goes through its life again, which the sentence does not suggest.

questions.s: The passage is mainly concerned with
o: why most Urdu newspapers chose Naskh over Nastaliq for most of the century.
how a typesetting system finally met the demands of the Nastaliq script.
the training that calligraphers received in the offices of the large dailies.
the history of the newspaper Jang from its founding up to the present day.
questions.e: The passage explains why Nastaliq resisted metal type and how Noori Nastaliq solved the problem. It says only some publishers switched to Naskh while most newspapers kept their katibs, and Jang appears only as an early adopter.

questions.s: According to the passage, metal type produced unsatisfactory Nastaliq mainly because
o: words built from separate letter pieces never joined naturally.
it could only print in the Naskh style used for much Arabic.
the metal pieces wore out faster than the katibs' pens did.
readers objected to the cost of newspapers printed with type.
questions.e: The second paragraph says founders set separate pieces for each letter form side by side, but the joins never looked natural. Some publishers chose to use Naskh, which shows that metal type could print it, not that it could print only Naskh.

questions.s: The remark that Noori Nastaliq looked like a katib's work "because, in a sense, it was" refers to the fact that
o: katibs went on copying out each page after the type had been set.
its ligatures had been written out by hand by a skilled calligrapher.
the computer was programmed to copy the slips made by tired writers.
Jang hired its former katibs to operate the new typesetting machines.
questions.e: Ahmed Mirza Jamil, a calligrapher, wrote the thousands of ligatures by hand, so every printed word was built from genuine calligraphy. The passage says the katib profession declined, which rules out katibs continuing to copy pages.

questions.s: The author's attitude toward the decline of the newspaper katib is best described as
o: indifferent, since the katibs' work had been slow and costly.
angry at the Urdu press for adopting computer typesetting.
relieved that readers no longer rely on handwritten pages.
regretful, while still regarding the new system as a success.
questions.e: The author writes that "Something was lost", naming the decline of everyday craftsmanship, but then calls the technology a success that satisfied readers. That sense of loss rules out indifference, and the praise for the system rules out anger.

questions.s: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
o: A reward tied to a measure fails once people can move the measure without serving the goal.
Perverse incentives arise mainly because many workers are willing to cheat for extra money.
Paying factory workers for each item they finish is the most reliable way to raise quality.
Hospitals should stop recording how long patients wait before they are given treatment.
questions.e: The second paragraph states the common thread: rewards work while the measure and the goal move together and fail once they come apart. The third paragraph explicitly says this is not usually a story about dishonesty.

questions.s: According to the passage, some patients were left waiting in ambulances because
o: the hospital's timing began only when patients reached the ward.
the hospital lacked enough ambulances to bring them in quickly.
the hospital was rewarded for the number of patients it refused.
the hospital was judged on how fast its ambulances had arrived.
questions.e: The hospital could record only the time from arrival in the ward to first attention, so keeping patients outside kept the clock from starting. The measure concerned treatment in the ward, not ambulance speed.

questions.s: The author discusses the teacher in the third paragraph mainly to
o: argue that teachers who prepare pupils for examinations are cheating.
give an example of an incentive that worked exactly as it was intended.
suggest that no teacher's salary should depend on any kind of measure.
show that responding to a flawed incentive need not be dishonest.
questions.e: The author says the teacher "is not cheating" but responding sensibly to the signal sent, placing the fault on the system. The final paragraph proposes better measures, not abandoning measurement altogether.

questions.s: Based on the passage, which reward scheme would the author most likely consider hardest to game?
o: One that pays a bonus for every item a worker finishes in a shift
One that pays residents for each rat tail they hand in to an office
One that judges a teacher by her pupils' marks in one examination
One that rewards output only if quality and complaints also improve
questions.e: The fourth paragraph recommends measuring several things at once so that improving one at the expense of the others brings no reward. Each of the other schemes rests on a single narrow number, the pattern the passage blames for perverse incentives.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Tapping songs on a desk is an effective way to teach music to young beginners.
Experts usually explain ideas more clearly than classmates who have just learned them.
Warning experts about their biases is the best way to improve the instructions they write.
People who know something often misjudge how hard it is for others to grasp.
questions.e: The tapping experiment and the later examples all show knowers overestimating what others will understand. The fourth paragraph says warnings do surprisingly little, so they are not the best remedy.

questions.s: According to the passage, tappers overestimate listeners' success because
o: they tap the rhythm too fast for listeners to follow it with any ease.
they choose songs that most of the listeners have never heard at all.
they hear the melody in their heads, while listeners hear only knocks.
they are told in advance that listeners guess about half of the songs.
questions.e: The second paragraph says the gap is not caused by poor tapping: the melody plays in the tapper's head, but the listener hears only a series of knocks. The figure of half is the tappers' own prediction, not something they are told.

questions.s: Based on the fourth paragraph, which step would most likely help an engineer design clearer controls?
o: Reading a detailed report on how the curse of knowledge works
Watching people who have never used the device try to operate it
Asking fellow engineers on the design team to review the controls
Adding technical terms so that every function is precisely named
questions.e: The paragraph says direct contact with a real beginner helps more than being told about the bias. Fellow engineers share the same knowledge, so their review would not reveal the gap.

questions.s: The final paragraph mainly serves to
o: argue that teachers should stop studying their subjects in depth.
describe a study comparing explanations by teachers and pupils.
apply the idea to teaching and suggest why a peer may explain better.
question whether the curse of knowledge exists beyond the classroom.
questions.e: The paragraph turns the idea toward teachers, noting that deep knowledge may make them forget early difficulty, which is why a classmate's explanation can help. It reports no study, and it treats the effect as real rather than doubting it.

questions.s: Which choice best describes the passage as a whole?
o: A young woman teaches an old letter-writer how to send messages on a mobile phone.
A letter-writer whose trade is fading finds his skill valued by an unexpected customer.
A letter-writer gives up his table and takes the shop job his nephew has offered him.
A farmer and his estranged brother settle an old quarrel with a professional's help.
questions.e: The passage shows Rahim Bakhsh losing customers to phones and then being sought out by a young woman who could text but wants his style. The nephew's offer is mentioned, but he is still at his table writing at the end.

questions.s: According to the passage, Rahim Bakhsh put the request for forgiveness at the end of the farmer's letter so that
o: the farmer's news about the harvest would seem more important.
the brother could ignore it without awkwardness if he wished.
it would fit into the space left at the bottom of the airmail page.
the brother would be sure to read it before anything else.
questions.e: The second paragraph says he wrote it last, in a single sentence, so that the brother could pretend not to have noticed it if he chose. Placing it last makes it easy to pass over, the opposite of making sure it is read first.

questions.s: Based on the passage, the girl most likely wants a handwritten letter because
o: she wants the words read aloud to her grandmother to sound careful and fitting.
her grandmother's neighbour does not know how to read messages on a phone.
a letter would reach Gujrat sooner than a message sent from her phone.
her grandmother has asked her never to send any messages by phone.
questions.e: She says she could send a message in a second but wants the grandmother to hear it "the way you write", "Properly", which points to the quality of the words, not the medium. Nothing suggests the neighbour cannot read a phone; the passage says she reads out whatever comes.

questions.s: The detail that Rahim Bakhsh leaves "space at the bottom of the page" mainly suggests that he
o: has run short of the blue airmail paper he usually writes on.
expects customers to discover more they want to say as he writes.
plans to add his own advice to the grandmother at the end.
intends to charge the girl extra for each additional line.
questions.e: The space is for "whatever the girl had not yet thought to say", echoing his early lesson that customers rarely know at first what they want to say. Nothing in the passage connects the space to his own advice or to payment.

questions.s: The passage is primarily concerned with
o: why Balochistan receives less rain than other provinces.
how electric tube wells are built and kept running by farmers.
how the karez works and why many of them have declined.
the history of wheat farming in the valleys of Balochistan.
questions.e: The passage explains the karez's construction and advantages, then how tube wells lowered the water table and dried many of them up. Rainfall and tube-well construction are background details, not the subject.

questions.s: According to the passage, one purpose of the vertical shafts is to
o: pump groundwater up from below the mother well.
store water for the hottest months of the summer.
let diggers remove soil and let air into the tunnel.
mark the boundaries between families' fields.
questions.e: The second paragraph says the shafts let diggers remove soil and let in air, and later serve as access points for cleaning. The karez works by gravity, so nothing in it is pumped.

questions.s: Based on the passage, a karez is most likely to keep flowing in a valley where
o: the tunnel is dug at a steep slope so that the water flows faster.
the vertical shafts are filled in once the tunnel has been finished.
the open channel at the lower end is made longer and much wider.
farmers draw little water from wells that reach deeper than the channel.
questions.e: A karez can deliver only what the groundwater provides, and deep pumping lowered the water table and dried many up, so little deep pumping protects its flow. A steep slope would make the water run fast enough to wear away the walls, which the builders avoid.

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage suggests that restoring a karez depends partly on
o: neighbours agreeing among themselves to limit pumping.
digging new tunnels deeper than the original ones.
replacing gravity flow with electric or diesel pumps.
finding new sources of rain in the nearby mountains.
questions.e: The sentence says success may depend less on digging than on whether neighbours agree to pump less, because pumping is what lowered the water table. Adding pumps would worsen the problem the passage describes.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Al-Biruni's result was more accurate than any modern measurement of the radius of the Earth.
Earlier astronomers proved that the Earth was curved by travelling across the Salt Range.
Al-Biruni's measurement was worthless, since the dip angle he relied on was so very small.
Al-Biruni's method mattered because it let one observer answer a question about the whole planet.
questions.e: The final paragraph says the measurement's importance lies in turning the Earth's size into a problem of reasoning that one observer could solve from a hilltop. The small dip angle is raised as a source of possible error, but the author explicitly says the importance does not depend on exactness.

questions.s: According to the passage, what did al-Biruni measure while standing on the summit?
o: How far the horizon dipped below the horizontal
The angle of the sun at noon on that same day
The distance from the hill to the fort of Nandana
The height of the hill above the plain below it
questions.e: The second paragraph says that on the summit he measured the dip of the horizon. He found the hill's height earlier, by sighting its top from two points on the ground.

questions.s: Based on the passage, al-Biruni's method would give no useful result if the observer
o: carried out the measurement alone, without any helpers.
found the hill's height by sighting it from two points.
used simple instruments rather than elaborate ones.
stood on ground no higher than the surrounding plain.
questions.e: The dip of the horizon grows with the observer's height, so at no height above the plain there would be no measurable dip and nothing to solve for. The passage stresses that a single observer with simple instruments was enough.

questions.s: The third paragraph mainly serves to
o: show that al-Biruni deliberately altered his figure to agree with earlier ones.
temper praise for the result by noting how small errors could have affected it.
explain in detail how the atmosphere makes the horizon look closer than it is.
suggest that the modern figure for the Earth's radius is less reliable than his.
questions.e: After calling the result remarkably close, the paragraph notes that a small dip angle and atmospheric bending mean some of the accuracy may be luck. It mentions the atmosphere's effect only briefly, as one reason for caution, without explaining it in detail.

questions.s: The passage mainly
o: argues that Cerdà's grid should be replaced by an entirely new street plan.
explains why Barcelona's medieval streets were too narrow for modern traffic.
describes the superblock idea, how it was received and a doubt that remains.
compares Barcelona's superblocks with similar schemes in several other cities.
questions.e: The passage explains how superblocks work, traces the move from early complaints to wider adoption, and ends with the concern about traffic pushed to the edges. It keeps Cerdà's grid and adapts it, and it mentions no other cities.

questions.s: According to the passage, which vehicles may still use the streets inside a superblock?
o: Any vehicle, provided that it travels at walking speed
Only buses and taxis that are crossing the district
Only bicycles and vehicles that belong to residents
Residents' vehicles, deliveries and emergency services
questions.e: The second paragraph lists residents' vehicles, deliveries and emergency services, all at walking speed. Walking speed is a condition on those vehicles, not permission for any vehicle, since through traffic is kept to the outer roads.

questions.s: The passage suggests that the later superblocks differed from the first one mainly in that
o: buildings were demolished to make room for squares.
through traffic was allowed back onto inner streets.
residents were consulted more before the work began.
the changes were designed to be costly and permanent.
questions.e: The fourth paragraph says the city extended the approach "this time with more public consultation", answering Poblenou residents' complaint that they had not been consulted. Nothing suggests the method changed to demolition or permanent works.

questions.s: The phrase "what it does not require" in the third paragraph refers mainly to
o: the fact that residents did not need to own cars to live in the area.
the lack of any studies of air pollution before the scheme began.
the decision not to consult residents before the first superblock.
the absence of demolition and road building in carrying out the scheme.
questions.e: The next sentence explains the phrase: no buildings were demolished and no new roads built, so the scheme was cheap and reversible. The lack of consultation was a drawback raised by critics, not part of the idea's appeal.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Stepwells were built chiefly as decorative monuments through which wealthy patrons displayed their piety to travellers.
Stepwells served practical, social and symbolic ends, and reviving them depends on the water that once sustained them.
Colonial officials destroyed most of the region's stepwells because they believed standing water spread disease.
Modern conservation work has returned water to most stepwells in the region and revived their public role.
questions.e: The passage moves from the engineering of stepwells to their social and symbolic uses and ends with the problem that restoration needs water, so this choice covers the whole text. The patrons' piety is only one detail of the second paragraph, and the colonial explanation is called incomplete, not the whole story.

questions.s: According to the passage, one reason stepwells became gathering places was that
o: caravans were forbidden to rest anywhere else in the towns
patrons handed out food to visitors who stopped to pray
they were designed from the start as markets for traders
the air near the water stayed cooler than at ground level
questions.e: The second paragraph states that the air near the water stays several degrees cooler, which made the shaded galleries resting and meeting places. The passage mentions shrines and lamp niches but says nothing about food, markets or rules for caravans.

questions.s: The author mentions the inscription on a Punjab baoli mainly to
o: suggest that a patron's charity could also advance the patron's own standing
prove that the stepwell was built during the Mughal period of the region's history
explain why local communities later abandoned many stepwells
show that women were the main users of stepwells in the Punjab
questions.e: The inscription asks drinkers to remember the builder, and the author draws the lesson that charity and self-promotion were rarely separate. The passage gives no date for the inscription, so it cannot be used as proof of a period.

questions.s: In the final sentence, the comparison of a dry, restored stepwell to "a stage set" suggests that such a building would
o: attract more visitors than a stepwell that still holds water
be easier and cheaper to maintain than the original structure
keep the appearance of the original while losing its function
be best suited to performances arranged by local theatre groups
questions.e: A stage set looks like a real place but does not work as one, so the comparison means the building would look right without doing what a stepwell does, which is to give access to water. Choosing the theatre option takes the metaphor literally.

questions.s: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?
o: It presents a scientific dispute, weighs the evidence on each side and then declares one hypothesis to be correct.
It traces the evolutionary history of one glowing species from its first appearance in the sea up to the present day.
It compares light production in marine and land organisms and argues that the marine forms are more advanced.
It opens with a familiar sight, explains the shared chemistry, considers why organisms glow and notes how research proceeds.
questions.e: The four paragraphs move from the glowing wake to the luciferin reaction, then to the purposes of light, then to the difficulty of research, which is what this choice describes. The passage does not declare the burglar alarm hypothesis correct; it ends by saying new recordings add uses rather than settle arguments.

questions.s: According to the passage, most bioluminescence in the sea is blue-green because
o: blue-green light travels farther through seawater than other colours do
luciferase can release energy only at blue and green wavelengths
red light would draw the attention of predators near the surface
dinoflagellates absorb every other colour from the water that surrounds them
questions.e: The second paragraph links the colour directly to the fact that blue-green light travels farthest through seawater. The passage says water absorbs red light, not dinoflagellates, and it makes no claim that the enzyme limits the colour.

questions.s: In the third paragraph, "the enemy of one's enemy" refers to
o: the crustaceans that feed on dinoflagellates
neighbouring dinoflagellates that flash in reply
the larger fish that hunt the dinoflagellates' grazers
the scientists who film glowing animals in the deep ocean
questions.e: The grazing crustaceans are the dinoflagellate's enemy, and the fish that hunt those crustaceans are the enemy of that enemy, so the flash calls the fish. Picking the crustaceans confuses the enemy with the one being summoned.

questions.s: The passage suggests that cameras on remotely operated vehicles are valuable mainly because they
o: give off enough light to make faint glows easier to measure
let scientists watch animals in their habitat rather than after capture
can bring deep-sea animals up from the dark ocean floor without harming them
have at last settled the long debate over the burglar alarm hypothesis
questions.e: The last paragraph says captured animals often stop glowing or die, so cameras that record behaviour where it happens solve that problem. The passage states that new recordings add uses rather than settle arguments, which rules out the debate option.

questions.s: The main purpose of the passage is to
o: argue that commission agents should be banned from lending any money to farmers
describe how banks in the Punjab calculate the interest on farm loans
explain why farmers use costly informal credit and what that means for policy
show that a 2018 survey overturned all earlier research on rural credit
questions.e: The passage explains the hidden advantages of the arhti's loans, admits their unfairness and ends with a lesson for policy, so explaining the choice and its policy meaning is the purpose. The author never calls for a ban; the conclusion is that formal credit must compete better.

questions.s: According to the passage, one advantage of the arhti's loans over bank loans is that they
o: always carry lower interest rates than bank loans
can be obtained the same day without formal paperwork
require the farmer to offer land titles as security
allow the farmer to sell the harvest to whichever buyer he likes
questions.e: The second paragraph contrasts weeks of bank paperwork with cash the same afternoon from the arhti. The passage says informal lenders charge far more than banks, and land titles are a bank requirement, so those choices reverse the facts.

questions.s: The findings of the 2018 survey are presented chiefly to support the claim that
o: informal lenders judge a borrower's reliability better than banks do
formal credit is generally too slow to be of real use to farmers
most indebted farmers eventually repay their commission agents in full
being tied to one lender who is also the buyer can cost farmers money
questions.e: The survey comes right after the point that a tied farmer cannot shop around, and it shows indebted farmers getting lower prices, which supports that claim. The point about judging reliability belongs to the previous paragraph and is not what the survey measured.

questions.s: As used in the passage, "complicated" most nearly means
o: disproved
confused
made less simple
made worse
questions.e: Later research added factors such as travel, delay and flexibility that made the earlier view look too simple. It did not disprove that view, since the third paragraph still says the arrangement is not fair.

questions.s: Which choice best summarises the passage?
o: Truck art is a personal, working tradition passed on by apprenticeship, and its wider fame draws mixed reactions.
Truck art first appeared in galleries abroad and was only later taken up by drivers and truck owners across Pakistan.
Truck owners decorate their vehicles mainly because transport rules require them to be clearly marked.
Truck painting is a dying craft, since young people in Pakistan no longer wish to spend years learning it.
questions.e: The passage covers the reasons for decoration, the training of painters and the mixed response to the art's new popularity, which this choice sums up. The galleries came later, not first, and the passage describes apprenticeships as continuing, not dying out.

questions.s: The author describes the truck as "a diary that happens to move" mainly to suggest that its decoration
o: records the routes and timetables the driver follows
was added little by little during the driver's years of travel
expresses the hopes and feelings of those who live with it
is meant to be read aloud by the passengers on board
questions.e: The sentence follows the examples of prayers for safety and couplets about love and loneliness, so the diary stands for personal feeling. The passage says decoration is done in a workshop over weeks, so the idea of slow addition during travel has no support.

questions.s: According to the passage, speed matters in the workshop because
o: paint dries very quickly in the heat of the workshops
the owner earns nothing while the truck is being painted
apprentices are paid only for the panels that they finish
customers judge painters mainly by how fast they work
questions.e: The third paragraph says every day in the workshop is a day without income for the owner. None of the other reasons is mentioned in the passage.

questions.s: In the final paragraph, the author treats the two reactions to truck art's new popularity by
o: dismissing the painters' worries as mere nostalgia for the past
arguing that commercial success will soon destroy the art form
preferring gallery shows to decorated cushions and teacups
presenting both and naming a point on which they agree
questions.e: The author reports the welcoming view and the worried view without judging them, then says both recognise the same fact. Nothing in the paragraph dismisses the worry or predicts that the art will be destroyed.

questions.s: The passage is mainly concerned with
o: persuading readers to stop buying the many products that contain lithium batteries
explaining how a lithium-ion battery stores electrical energy and then releases it
comparing ways of recovering battery materials and what each of them requires
celebrating the success of direct recycling in battery factories around the world
questions.e: The second and third paragraphs set out three recovery methods with their strengths and weaknesses, and the last paragraph names the conditions a recycling industry needs. The passage lists what a battery contains but never explains how it stores energy, so that option describes a detail, not the focus.

questions.s: According to the passage, one drawback of smelting is that
o: much of the lithium ends up in slag that is costly to process
it can accept batteries of only one design at a time
it produces large volumes of acidic liquid waste
it destroys the copper and aluminium in each battery
questions.e: The second paragraph says lithium tends to end up in the slag, from which it is costly to retrieve. Acidic liquid waste is the drawback of the second, acid-based method, and smelting is praised for accepting many designs at once.

questions.s: Based on the passage, which development would most help direct recycling become practical on a large scale?
o: Furnaces that reach higher temperatures while burning less fuel
Stronger acids that dissolve black mass more quickly and fully
More small workshops that take old batteries apart by hand
Collecting and sorting old batteries by chemistry before processing
questions.e: Direct recycling works best when incoming batteries share the same chemistry, so sorting them by chemistry removes its main weakness. Furnaces and acids belong to the other two methods and would not help direct recycling at all.

questions.s: As used in the passage, "fussiness" refers to direct recycling's
o: slowness compared with the older methods
need for input that is all of one kind
tendency to start fires in small workshops
high cost of the chemicals that it uses
questions.e: The sentence explains the word at once: the method works best when the batteries share the same chemistry. Fires are a danger of hand dismantling in workshops, not of direct recycling.

questions.s: Which choice best describes what happens in the passage?
o: A grandmother agrees to sell her shop to a young man who plans to scan and reprint old books.
After a visitor's offer, a girl trained by her grandmother is trusted with a difficult repair.
A student brings her damaged chemistry book to a bookbinder and learns to repair it herself.
A girl persuades her grandmother to modernise the family business by buying a new phone.
questions.e: The story builds Sana's training, brings in the young man's offer and ends with Nani handing Sana the worst repair without watching her. Nani never agrees to sell anything, and the chemistry book belongs to a customer, not to Sana.

questions.s: According to the passage, what did Sana's grandmother do when Sana made a wrong stitch?
o: She scolded Sana in front of the customers.
She redid the stitch herself without a word.
She cut out the stitch and returned the needle.
She sent Sana home for the rest of the day.
questions.e: The second paragraph says she simply cut the stitch out and handed the needle back. Redoing the stitch herself is tempting because she says nothing, but the passage stresses that Sana had to do it again.

questions.s: Nani's question "who will mend it?" most strongly suggests that she
o: doubts that the young man's business values the work of repair
wants to bargain for a higher price for her marbled paper
fears the young man will open a rival repair shop in the lane
believes printed copies will last longer than the old books
questions.e: Nani's question points to what happens when a copy fails, and the young man's answer that they would simply print another confirms that repair has no place in his plan. Nothing in the scene shows her bargaining over the price.

questions.s: The final sentence ("for the first time her grandmother did not watch her hands") mainly suggests that
o: the grandmother has lost interest in the shop since the offer
the grandmother is too tired to supervise Sana's work any longer
Sana has made mistakes that her grandmother now chooses to ignore
Sana has finally earned her grandmother's trust in the craft
questions.e: Earlier, Nani checked every stitch; not watching now, just after handing over the worst repair, signals trust. The idea that she has lost interest ignores that she chose this moment to give Sana a harder task.

questions.s: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
o: Replanting campaigns have fully solved the problems that upstream irrigation caused in the delta.
The grey mangrove is the only tree species able to survive in salty and waterlogged coastal soil.
Coastal families have left the delta mainly because mangrove wood is no longer easy to obtain.
The delta's mangroves are valuable, but their future depends on river flow as well as planting.
questions.e: The passage praises the mangroves' value, explains the damage done by reduced river flow and ends with ecologists warning that planting alone is not enough. The replanting option ignores that caution, and the passage blames families' departure on seawater, not on a shortage of wood.

questions.s: According to the passage, the grey mangrove copes with salt by
o: storing it in the breathing roots under the mud
releasing it through glands in its leaves
growing only in creeks fed by fresh water
shedding its leaves each time the tide rises
questions.e: The first paragraph says the tree gets rid of excess salt through glands in its leaves. The breathing roots are mentioned in the same sentence, but they take in air rather than store salt.

questions.s: The statement that "even a tolerant species has limits" implies that
o: the grey mangrove can withstand rising salinity only up to a point
camels have harmed more mangroves than salt water has
other mangrove species would be better suited to the delta
mangroves can no longer grow anywhere on the Sindh coast
questions.e: The phrase follows the point that creeks grow saltier without fresh water, so it means the salt-tolerant mangrove can survive only so much salt. The final paragraph reports that cover has grown, which rules out the idea that mangroves can no longer grow there.

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage serves mainly to
o: recommend planting new mangrove forests along the upper course of the river
praise the planters whose efforts can now be seen in satellite images
suggest that the coastal forest's health depends on the river far inland
argue that every dam on the river should be removed as soon as possible
questions.e: Calling the mangrove belt the visible edge of a system whose engine lies upstream means that the forest depends on how much water and silt the river delivers. Mangroves grow in salt water at the coast, so planting them upstream makes no sense, and the passage never calls for removing dams.

questions.s: The primary purpose of the passage is to
o: describe the career and discoveries of an eighteenth-century French astronomer
argue that plants respond to sunlight more quickly than animals are able to
explain what plants' internal clocks are and how they benefit plants
show that the internal clock of a plant runs at exactly twenty-four hours
questions.e: De Mairan's experiment only opens the passage, which then explains how plant clocks work, what they let plants do and how a matched clock aids growth. The passage says the clock runs at about twenty-four hours and drifts, so the option claiming exactly twenty-four hours contradicts it.

questions.s: The comparison with "a slightly inaccurate watch" mainly illustrates how
o: scientists first measured the precise length of a plant's internal cycle
the clocks of plants keep better time than the clocks of people
plants are unable to keep any kind of time in constant darkness
daily light and temperature reset a clock that would otherwise drift
questions.e: The watch is corrected each morning against a signal, just as the plant clock, which drifts on its own, is reset by dawn light and temperature. De Mairan's cupboard showed that plants do keep time in darkness, so that option reverses the evidence.

questions.s: The example of starch use at night suggests that plants
o: store much more starch in winter than they do in summer
match their nightly use of reserves to the expected length of night
stop all of their activity during the hours of darkness
cannot photosynthesise until their stored starch has run out
questions.e: The plant uses starch at a rate that leaves only a small reserve by dawn, as though it had calculated the length of the night. Using starch is itself activity, so the claim that plants stop all activity at night contradicts the example.

questions.s: Based on the experiments described in the final paragraph, a plant whose clock runs on a cycle of about twenty hours would most likely grow best in
o: an artificial day lasting close to twenty hours
a natural day of twenty-four hours, like the real one
constant light, which removes any need for a clock
any day length at all, since dawn resets the clock
questions.e: The experiments found that plants grew best when the artificial day matched their internal cycle, so a twenty-hour clock suits a twenty-hour day. The twenty-four-hour option is tempting because it is the natural day, but it would leave this plant mismatched.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Gandharan artists combined borrowed techniques with local stories to create a distinct art.
Gandhara was, beyond any doubt, the first place where the Buddha was shown in human form.
Gandharan sculptors copied Greek statues closely and then simply added Buddhist names to them.
Buddhist art lost its quality once it left Gandhara and travelled on to Central Asia and China.
questions.e: The passage stresses that Gandharan sculptors borrowed drapery and portraiture but used them for local subjects, forming a new visual language. It says the question of who first showed the Buddha in human form may never be settled, so the 'beyond any doubt' option contradicts it.

questions.s: According to the passage, early Buddhist reliefs indicated the Buddha's presence through
o: portraits modelled on the faces of Kushan rulers
carvings of travelling monks and merchants
symbols such as footprints and an empty seat
figures dressed in Greek and Roman robes
questions.e: The second paragraph lists footprints, an empty seat beneath a tree and a wheel as the symbols used before the Buddha was shown as a man. Robes in the Mediterranean style belong to the later Gandharan figures, not to the early reliefs.

questions.s: The passage suggests that the debate over whether Gandhara or Mathura first showed the Buddha in human form continues mainly because
o: the two regions produced their images in exactly the same style
few sculptures from either region can be dated with confidence
Kushan rulers forbade any images of the Buddha in Mathura
historians disagree about where the region of Gandhara lay
questions.e: The author says the question may never be settled because few pieces from either region carry reliable dates. The passage describes Mathura's style as quite different and fuller-bodied, so the same-style option is wrong.

questions.s: The author's attitude toward the label "Greco-Buddhist" is best described as
o: enthusiastic approval
complete indifference
angry rejection
measured scepticism
questions.e: The author says such labels 'can' mislead and explains why, which is a reasoned doubt rather than an outburst. Angry rejection overstates a calm, qualified objection.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Most workers are unwilling to save for their old age under any kind of arrangement.
Firms should never offer savings plans that employees have to join by their own choice.
Automatic enrolment always leads workers to save enough money for a secure retirement.
How a savings choice is presented strongly affects what people do, for good and ill.
questions.e: The passage shows that switching the default raises saving sharply, then warns that defaults can also keep contributions too low, so the effect cuts both ways. The fourth paragraph directly contradicts the claim that automatic enrolment always produces enough saving.

questions.s: In the textile firm example, the change that raised participation was that
o: new workers were enrolled unless they chose to leave
the firm began to match the amount each worker saved
the share of salary paid into the plan was increased
new workers attended a talk about planning for retirement
questions.e: The passage says the firm reversed the arrangement so that workers were enrolled automatically, and that nothing else changed. The matching payment existed from the start, so it cannot explain the rise.

questions.s: The third paragraph suggests that enrolled workers are reluctant to leave the plan partly because
o: the firm charges a fee to anyone who withdraws from it
they have never been told that leaving is permitted
giving up the savings feels like losing something they own
the form for leaving is much longer than the form for joining
questions.e: The paragraph says people come to regard the savings as already theirs, so leaving feels like a loss rather than a missed gain. The passage mentions a form to leave but never compares its length with the joining form.

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage mainly serves to
o: argue that workers should be left to design their own savings plans
stress that those who design choices cannot avoid shaping decisions
suggest that automatic enrolment ought to be abolished altogether
claim that the textile firm acted irresponsibly in changing its plan
questions.e: Since there is no neutral way to present an option, whoever sets up the choice influences the outcome and so bears responsibility. The author proposes improving defaults with automatic increases, not abolishing them.

questions.s: Which choice best summarises the passage?
o: A retired teacher gives up his letters after most go unanswered and turns to the internet.
A retired teacher keeps writing to old pupils and is rewarded with a reply from one of them.
A former pupil returns to Multan to thank the teacher who once made him stand in class.
A daughter-in-law helps her father-in-law trace his former pupils who now live abroad.
questions.e: Master Iqbal ignores the suggestion to use the internet, keeps writing, receives the engineer's letter and goes on to the next name. The engineer writes from Toronto; he does not come back to Multan.

questions.s: Master Iqbal's response to letters stamped "unknown" suggests that he
o: blames the post office for losing the letters he has sent
suspects that his former pupils are ignoring him on purpose
decides to write only to the pupils he remembers fondly
accepts disappointment calmly and carries on with his task
questions.e: He does not take returned letters as rebukes; he crosses out the address and moves to the next name. The passage gives no sign that he blames anyone, and he continues down the whole ledger rather than choosing favourites.

questions.s: According to the passage, the engineer remembered being made to explain
o: why a triangle holds its shape and a square does not
how to draw an aeroplane accurately and to scale
how a bridge is designed to carry heavy loads
why his exercise books should be kept neat
questions.e: The engineer recalls standing by the blackboard until he could explain why a triangle holds its shape and a square does not. He designs bridges now, but that is his career, not the lesson he was made to explain.

questions.s: Master Iqbal's adding "built bridges" beneath the old note about aeroplanes mainly suggests that he
o: regrets having been so strict with the boy many years ago
wants to correct an error he once made in the ledger
values learning how the boy he remembered turned out as a man
plans to write next to the engineer's students in Toronto
questions.e: He keeps the old line and adds the new one beneath it, joining the boy he taught to the man he became, after reading the letter three times. Nothing suggests the old note was an error; the engineer himself admits he drew aeroplanes.

questions.s: The main purpose of the passage is to
o: argue that phone makers should fit an atomic clock inside every new device
describe the history of the satellite launches that created the system
explain how a receiver uses timed signals to work out its position precisely
warn that satellite positioning is too unreliable to be trusted in large cities
questions.e: Each paragraph explains part of the method: timing signals, the role of four satellites, the precision needed and the remaining errors. The passage mentions errors from tall buildings but says software now handles many of them, so it does not warn readers off the system.

questions.s: According to the passage, a receiver uses a fourth satellite in order to
o: see past the tall buildings that block signals in a city
download the map that is displayed on the phone's screen
measure the delay caused by the upper atmosphere
work out the error in its own clock as well as its position
questions.e: Three distances would fix the position if the phone's clock were perfect, but its cheap quartz clock is not, so a fourth signal lets it solve for the clock error too. The passage says the phone only listens for time signals; it never says satellites send maps.

questions.s: Based on the figures in the passage, a timing error of one ten-millionth of a second would misplace a position by about
o: 3 metres
30 metres
300 metres
3 kilometres
questions.e: A millionth of a second gives about 300 metres, and a ten-millionth is one tenth of that, so the error is about 30 metres (light covers 30 cm per billionth of a second, and 100 billionths × 30 cm = 30 m). Choosing 300 metres repeats the passage's figure without scaling it down.

questions.s: As used in the passage, "severe" most nearly means
o: demanding
cruel
solemn
violent
questions.e: The sentence introduces how exact the timing must be, so 'severe' means strict or demanding. 'Cruel' and 'violent' fit the word's use for people or storms, not for a requirement.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The cleaning of the Sistine Chapel ceiling was a mistake that did lasting harm to Michelangelo's work.
Modern scientific equipment has removed all of the uncertainty from the restoration of old paintings.
Conservators in Lahore rely on methods that are quite different from those used by restorers in Rome.
