Restoring a painting requires hard judgements, which modern practice handles with caution and reversibility.
questions.e: The passage presents the question of what counts as the real work and then shows how testing, records and reversible methods manage it. The author says the Sistine dispute was never resolved, so calling the cleaning a mistake goes beyond the text.

questions.s: The author mentions the dispute over the Sistine Chapel ceiling mainly to
o: argue that Michelangelo used brighter colours than other painters of his time
introduce a dilemma that conservators of paintings face in general
criticise the visitors who preferred the ceiling before it was cleaned
show that restorers in Rome are more skilled than restorers elsewhere
questions.e: The first paragraph ends by saying the dispute illustrates a problem that every conservator faces, and the next paragraph explains that problem. The author reports both reactions to the cleaning without criticising either group of visitors.

questions.s: According to the passage, conservators prefer reversible methods because
o: a future restorer who knows more may need to undo the work
reversible materials are cheaper and quicker to apply
visitors often object to changes made to famous paintings
ultraviolet light slowly damages permanent fillings
questions.e: The third paragraph says a new filling should be removable by a future restorer who may know more. Ultraviolet light is mentioned only as a way of examining surfaces before cleaning.

questions.s: Which decision would the author most likely regard as sound conservation practice?
o: Repainting faded areas so that a wall looks exactly as it did when new
Removing every later layer at once to reach the original surface quickly
Filling a crack with a material that can later be removed without harm
Leaving a wall untouched even though trapped moisture is destroying it
questions.e: A removable filling preserves the work while leaving choices open for later restorers, which matches the principle in the final paragraph. Leaving a decaying wall alone fails the first half of that principle, to do what is needed to preserve the work.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Lahore is hotter than any other city in Pakistan because it has almost no trees left.
Cities trap heat, and small forests help most when combined with other measures.
Miyawaki forests have been shown to lower the temperature of whole districts of Lahore.
Critics argue that cities in hot climates should stop planting trees altogether.
questions.e: The passage explains the heat island, describes mini-forests and their limits, and ends by calling for a set of measures together. The critics say a small plot cannot cool a whole district, which is the opposite of the Miyawaki option.

questions.s: According to the passage, the urban heat island effect is usually strongest
o: at night
at midday
in winter
after rain
questions.e: The first paragraph says the effect is usually strongest at night, when stored heat is released. Midday is tempting because sunlight is strongest then, but the passage stresses the slow release after dark.

questions.s: The critics described in the third paragraph would most likely agree that
o: mini-forests should be replaced entirely by roofs that reflect sunlight
residents should be kept from taking part in the planting of trees
Miyawaki's method cannot succeed anywhere with a hot climate
the cooling effect of a single mini-forest is mostly local
questions.e: The critics say a tennis-court-sized plot cools its immediate surroundings but not a district, so its effect is local. They are described as not opposed to trees, so replacing the forests entirely goes too far.

questions.s: The final paragraph mainly serves to
o: declare that the critics have clearly won the debate over mini-forests
introduce a new problem that is caused by roofs that reflect sunlight
suggest that a combination of measures is needed to cool a city
summarise Miyawaki's original argument in favour of dense planting
questions.e: The paragraph says the debate shifts attention to a set of solutions that together do what no single project can. It includes many small forests in that set, so it does not side wholly with the critics.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Von Frisch's account of the waggle dance has now been shown to be entirely mistaken.
Honeybees find food chiefly by following the scents that their sisters carry home.
The waggle dance does carry information, but how much it helps depends on conditions.
Bees can see the dance clearly in spite of the darkness that fills the hive.
questions.e: The passage confirms that the dance encodes direction and distance, then reports that its benefit appears mainly when food is scarce and scattered. The final paragraph says the results do not diminish von Frisch's achievement, which rules out the 'entirely mistaken' option.

questions.s: Based on the passage, if a patch of flowers lies in exactly the direction of the sun, the dancer's waggle run on the comb would point
o: straight down
horizontally to the left
toward the hive entrance
straight up
questions.e: The angle of the run from straight up equals the angle between the food and the sun; if that angle is zero, the run points straight up. Straight down would mean the food lies directly away from the sun.

questions.s: In which situation would the researchers expect the largest difference in food gathered between colonies with normal dances and colonies with scrambled dances?
o: A spring meadow full of flowers right next to the hive
A dry season with a few flowering trees spread over a wide area
A garden with a single large flower bed beside the hive
A field of one crop in full bloom all around the hive
questions.e: The passage says the dance helped mainly when good flowers were scarce and scattered, which describes a dry season with a few distant trees. In the other three settings food is plentiful and close, where bees did nearly as well without readable dances.

questions.s: As used in the passage, "diminish" most nearly means
o: lessen
explain
repeat
conceal
questions.e: The author is saying that the new results do not make von Frisch's achievement any smaller, so 'diminish' means lessen. 'Conceal' would mean hiding the achievement, which is not what the sentence is about.

questions.s: The passage is primarily concerned with
o: tracing how the place-value system spread and why it was accepted slowly
proving that Fibonacci himself invented zero and the place-value system
arguing that Roman numerals are in fact better suited to keeping accounts
describing the life and long travels of the mathematician al-Khwarizmi
questions.e: The passage follows the system from India through Baghdad to Italy and then explains the obstacles to its adoption. Fibonacci only promoted the numerals in 1202, long after Brahmagupta's rules for zero, so he did not invent them.

questions.s: According to the passage, the word "algorithm" comes from
o: the title of Fibonacci's book on bookkeeping
a Latin word for the counting boards of merchants
a Latin form of the name of al-Khwarizmi
Brahmagupta's rules for calculating with zero
questions.e: The second paragraph says al-Khwarizmi's name, rendered in Latin as Algoritmi, gave European languages the word. Fibonacci's book is mentioned in the next sentence, which makes it a tempting but wrong choice.

questions.s: The passage suggests that counting boards slowed the adoption of the new numerals because
o: they could not be used together with Roman numerals
the city of Florence had banned their use by bankers
operating them required a knowledge of zero
people who calculated on them had little need for written arithmetic
questions.e: Since most calculation was done on boards and only results were written down, the advantage of numerals for written arithmetic mattered little until calculating on paper became common. Florence banned the new figures in account books, not counting boards.

questions.s: The final paragraph mainly serves to
o: introduce a new example of an invention that was adopted slowly
draw a general lesson from the history described in the passage
contradict the claim that the new numerals were truly superior
explain why paper became cheap in Europe in the later Middle Ages
questions.e: The paragraph turns the story of the numerals into a general point about how good ideas need tools, users and a reason to change. It accepts that the system was superior rather than contradicting it.

questions.s: Which choice best describes what the passage mainly does?
o: It defends Hardin's view that every shared resource must be turned into private property.
It presents Hardin's argument and then shows how Ostrom's research qualified it.
It describes the nets and boats used by fishing communities on the Makran coast.
It argues that control by the state is the surest way to protect the world's fish stocks.
questions.e: The first two paragraphs set out Hardin's argument, and the last two show Ostrom's evidence that communities can avoid the tragedy under certain conditions. The author does not defend Hardin's conclusion; the final sentence calls the tragedy a risk, not a law.

questions.s: According to Hardin's argument as described in the passage, each herder keeps adding animals because
o: the state encourages herders to keep increasing the size of their herds
no herder knows how much grass the shared pasture is able to support
the other herders have already agreed to reduce their own herds
he gains the whole benefit of each animal while the cost is shared
questions.e: Hardin's point is the imbalance between a private gain and a shared cost, which the first paragraph states directly. The state appears only in Hardin's proposed remedy, not as the cause of overgrazing.

questions.s: In the Makran example, outside trawlers threaten the local arrangement mainly because their crews
o: use much larger nets than the town's own boat owners use
fish only during the seasons that the town has agreed on
had no part in making the rules and face none of its penalties
are watched far too closely by members of the local community
questions.e: Ostrom's conditions include users who make the rules and penalties that apply to them, and the passage says the trawlers' crews took no part in the rules and face no penalties. Net size is never mentioned, so that option adds an idea the passage does not support.

questions.s: The author calls the tragedy of the commons "a risk under certain conditions rather than a law of nature" mainly to stress that it
o: can be avoided when the right arrangements are in place
can no longer happen in any modern fishing town
is caused mainly by natural disasters such as storms
affects herders on pastures but never affects fishing communities
questions.e: A law of nature always holds, while a risk depends on conditions, so the tragedy can be avoided where Ostrom's conditions are met. The author says Ostrom does not show the tragedy never happens, so 'no longer happen' overstates the point.

questions.s: Which choice best summarises the passage?
o: On a long train journey, a student meets a retired signalman whose talk stays with him.
A retired signalman travels south to visit the station in Karachi where he once worked for years.
A student helps a confused old man to find the right station during a long and delayed journey.
A physics student explains to an old railway worker how the modern signals on the line operate.
questions.e: The narrator meets the old man, hears about his work, struggles with a question about brakes and later opens his textbook, which this choice sums up. The old man gets off at a small station in Sindh, not in Karachi, and it is he who questions the student, not the reverse.

questions.s: According to the passage, the brass bell at the signalman's station rang when
o: a train was approaching the station from Karachi
the signalman's long shift had come to an end
a train left the station before his on the line
a passenger had been left behind on the platform
questions.e: The second paragraph says the bell rang when a train left the station before his. The passage does not say which direction trains came from, so the Karachi option adds a detail.

questions.s: The comparison with "a carpenter" describing tools "he no longer owned" suggests that the old man spoke about his former work
o: with bitterness at having been forced to retire too early
with plain, practical familiarity rather than longing
with pride in having built his own equipment by hand
with confusion about how the old signals had worked
questions.e: The sentence says he spoke without nostalgia, and a carpenter describing old tools speaks with exact, practical knowledge. Nothing in the passage suggests that he resented retiring or that he made his equipment.

questions.s: The final paragraph suggests that the narrator
o: has decided to train as a signalman once he finishes his studies
regrets that he did not ask the old man more about his life
believes the old man would be disappointed by his choice of subject
has been prompted by the talk to take his studies more seriously
questions.e: He had not meant to open the textbook, but after failing to explain how a train stops he opens it that afternoon and counts this as a result of the meeting. He says only that the old man might not have counted it as a result, which is not the same as disappointment.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The Himalaya were formed, and are still changing, because India is pushing into Asia.
The Himalaya will go on growing taller without any limit for as long as India moves north.
Mount Everest is the only mountain in the world on which fossils of sea creatures are found.
Earthquakes in Kashmir are caused mainly by rivers and glaciers wearing away the rock.
questions.e: The passage explains how the collision built the range and then shows that it continues, raising peaks and causing earthquakes. The third paragraph says the mountains do not grow taller without limit, because erosion balances uplift.

questions.s: According to the passage, neither India nor Asia sank beneath the other because
o: the ocean between them had already filled up with river sediment
both were made of continental rock too thick and buoyant to sink
India was moving far too slowly to force its way downward
the plateau of Tibet stood as a barrier between the two
questions.e: The second paragraph says both landmasses were made of thick, buoyant continental rock, unlike dense ocean floor, which does sink. Tibet was raised by the collision, so it could not have kept the two apart.

questions.s: The comparison with the growth of fingernails mainly helps readers
o: see why the collision is likely to end quite soon
understand how rivers wear rock away over time
picture how the crust was folded into sheets
grasp how slowly India is moving at present
questions.e: Fingernails grow at a few centimetres a year, so the comparison gives a familiar sense of India's slow northward movement. The passage states that the collision has not ended, which rules out the first option.

questions.s: Based on the passage, which change would most likely make the range grow higher over time if all other factors stayed the same?
o: A slowing of India's northward movement into Asia
A greater flow of sediment down to the Indus plains
A drier climate that reduced erosion by rivers and glaciers
A long pause in earthquakes along the plate boundary
questions.e: The height of the range reflects a balance between uplift and erosion, so reducing erosion while uplift continues would let the mountains rise. More sediment reaching the plains would mean more erosion, which works in the opposite direction.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Saraiki and Balochi have grammar that is far too complex for computers to translate well.
Companies have already built reliable translation tools for most of the languages of Pakistan.
Translation tools fail some languages mainly for lack of data, a problem with social sides too.
Training one system on many languages at once has fully solved the data shortage for rare languages.
questions.e: The passage says the gap comes from data, describes ways to ease the shortage and ends with the social question of who controls that data. The first paragraph explicitly denies that harder grammar is the main cause.

questions.s: According to the passage, today's translation systems are trained mainly on
o: sentences paired with their translations
dictionaries that list individual words
recordings of people's everyday spoken language
grammar rules written down by linguists
questions.e: The second paragraph says systems learn from parallel texts, sentences paired with their translations. Spoken language is mentioned as a reason data are scarce, not as training material.

questions.s: Which statement about training one system on many languages is best supported by the passage?
o: It works only when all of the languages involved share the same script.
It has removed any need to collect new sentences from native speakers.
It costs more than paying speakers to translate sets of sentences.
It should help most where a rare language has well-resourced relatives.
questions.e: The passage says learning can carry over to a related language and gives the example of Urdu and Punjabi helping with Saraiki, so relatedness is what makes the method useful. The passage presents speaker translation as a separate, still-needed approach, so the method has not removed that need.

questions.s: The final paragraph mainly serves to
o: describe a new technical method for translating spoken languages
raise the question of who should control a language's data
argue that younger speakers should give up their home languages
show that outside companies refuse to work on rare languages
questions.e: The paragraph moves from technique to ownership, ending with the claim that whose data it is matters as much as how much there is. It reports a worry that young speakers may abandon their languages; it does not urge them to.

questions.s: The main purpose of the passage is to
o: argue that children should begin to study physics at an earlier age
compare the climate of Gilgit with the climate of the city of Karachi
explain the physics behind the colours of the sky and of clouds
describe the life and scientific career of the physicist Lord Rayleigh
questions.e: After dismissing the sea explanation, the passage explains scattering and uses it to account for the blue sky, red sunsets and white clouds. Gilgit and Karachi appear only to show that the sea cannot be the cause, so comparing their climates is not the purpose.

questions.s: According to the passage, the sky does not look violet partly because
o: sunlight holds less violet than blue, and our eyes respond more to blue
violet light has a longer wavelength than blue light does
clouds absorb most of the violet light arriving from the sun
air molecules are too large to scatter violet light at all
questions.e: The third paragraph gives two reasons: sunlight contains less violet to begin with, and human eyes are more sensitive to blue. The passage says violet has a shorter wavelength than blue, so the second option reverses the fact.

questions.s: Based on the passage, an astronaut standing on the Moon, which has no atmosphere, would most likely see the daytime sky as
o: bright blue, since the sunlight there still contains blue light
white, like the clouds that form above Earth's cities
orange and red, as at sunset on Earth
black, since there is no air to scatter the sunlight
questions.e: The passage explains that the blue sky is light scattered by air molecules, so without air there is no scattered light and the sky away from the sun stays dark. Blue light reaches the Moon, but it is not scattered toward the viewer, so the first option misses the point.

questions.s: The author mentions the dust and smoke over cities in winter mainly to
o: warn readers about the health effects of breathing polluted air
give an everyday case of larger particles scattering all colours
show that the sky over Karachi is bluer than the sky over Gilgit
explain why sunsets in cities look redder than in the mountains
questions.e: The sentence follows the point that large particles scatter all colours roughly equally, and it shows that effect making a city sky pale. Health is never discussed, and the first paragraph says the mountain sky is often the bluer one.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The Grand Trunk Road was first built by the British during the nineteenth century.
A ruler with a short reign organised an old route to serve travellers and the state.
Sher Shah Suri ruled north India for longer than any of the Mughal emperors did.
The sarais along the road were built mainly so that they would grow into towns.
questions.e: The passage credits Sher Shah Suri with organising an ancient route through sarais, wells and messengers, and shows that this served government as well as travellers. The British only paved stretches and gave the name; the route existed two thousand years earlier.

questions.s: According to the passage, horses were kept ready at the sarais so that
o: merchants could carry their goods between market towns
travellers without transport could buy one on the way
the troops of the Mughal army could pull their carts
messengers could carry news quickly across the empire
questions.e: The second paragraph says the horses let messengers ride from one sarai to the next, carrying news and orders faster than before. Market towns grew up around the sarais later, but the horses are not linked to merchants' goods.

questions.s: The third paragraph mainly serves to
o: show that the road also served the ruler's political aims
describe daily life for the travellers who stayed in sarais
argue that Sher Shah Suri cared little for ordinary people
explain how the British later paved and straightened the road
questions.e: The paragraph begins by saying the motive was not only generosity and lists revenue, control of rebellion and oversight of governors. 'Not only' means the author accepts both motives, so the claim that he cared little for people overstates it.

questions.s: The final sentence suggests that Sher Shah Suri's legacy lies partly in
o: the modern name of the road, which he chose himself
the paving that gave the road its present surface
the way people on the route still think of a journey in stages
the separate quarters that modern hotels offer their guests
questions.e: The sentence calls the habit of measuring a journey by the distance between rest stops his legacy, which reflects his chain of sarais. The name Grand Trunk Road was given by the British, according to the same paragraph.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Many people in Pakistan have stopped drinking tea because its price has risen so sharply.
Kenya alone decides the price of tea in every country that imports tea from it.
Growing tea at home would quickly end Pakistan's need to import tea from abroad.
Imported and habit-bound, tea gets dearer when the rupee falls, and buyers adapt quietly.
questions.e: The passage explains why a weaker rupee passes into tea prices, how households adjust without stopping, and why policy has no quick fix. It says few people give up their morning cup, which contradicts the first option.

questions.s: As the passage uses the term, demand is "inelastic" when
o: prices stay fixed even though demand keeps rising
buyers switch quickly to a cheaper product instead
people keep buying about the same amount as prices rise
sellers refuse to raise prices for their loyal customers
questions.e: The second paragraph defines inelastic demand as people buying roughly the same amount even as the price rises. Switching to cheaper products is described later as a separate response, not as the meaning of the term.

questions.s: The passage suggests that national sales figures can give an incomplete picture because they
o: include the tea grown on a small scale in the hills of the north
may not reveal changes in what households buy and how they use it
are published only after the value of the rupee has recovered
count loose tea and branded tea as two quite separate products
questions.e: The third paragraph says switching brands, buying smaller packs and brewing leaves longer rarely show up as falling sales, though the changes are real. None of the other claims about the figures appears in the passage.

questions.s: The final paragraph mainly serves to
o: show that each possible policy response has costs or limits
recommend that import duties on tea be cut without delay
argue that efforts to grow tea locally have already failed
explain how the size of the Kenyan harvest is measured
questions.e: The paragraph pairs each option with a drawback: lower duties cut revenue, and local cultivation is slow and needs suitable land. The author presents duty cuts as a trade-off, not as a recommendation.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Qawwali is a devotional form whose performances build slowly and respond to listeners.
Qawwali was invented in the nineteenth century, when the harmonium first arrived from Europe.
Qawwali is sung only in the Persian language and must follow a fixed, carefully written score.
Qawwali lost all of its meaning once singers began to perform it in concert halls abroad.
questions.e: The passage describes qawwali's devotional roots, its gradual build and the way singers adapt each performance to the audience. Only the harmonium arrived in the nineteenth century; the form itself is traced back to Amir Khusrau centuries earlier.

questions.s: According to the passage, the technique called girah involves
o: repeating the opening line of the song until the audience starts to clap
adding a couplet from another poem that comments on the main text
switching from the harmonium to the tabla halfway through the song
translating the poem from Persian into Urdu during the performance
questions.e: The third paragraph defines girah as weaving in a couplet from a different poem that comments on the main text. Repeating a line is a separate technique mentioned just before it, which makes the first option tempting.

questions.s: The statement that the same song "may last ten minutes one evening and forty the next" mainly illustrates
o: how poorly many qawwali singers remember the words of long songs
the difference between performances at shrines and in concert halls
how much a performance depends on the singer's response to the audience
the slow tempo at which almost every qawwali performance begins
questions.e: The sentence ends a paragraph about singers watching the audience and repeating or adding lines as they react, so length varies with that response. The paragraph does not compare shrine and concert settings; that comes later.

questions.s: Based on the final paragraph, the purists and those who answered them would both most likely accept which statement?
o: Qawwali should never be performed anywhere outside a shrine.
Concert audiences understand qawwali better than shrine audiences.
Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan changed the poetry that qawwali uses.
The audience takes an active part in shaping a qawwali performance.
questions.e: The paragraph says both sides agreed that qawwali is a conversation between singer and audience. Only the purists might hold that it belongs in the shrine, so the first option is not shared by both.

questions.s: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Most of the plastic found in the ocean is thrown overboard directly from ships at sea.
A few giant rivers are now known to deliver nearly all of the plastic in the oceans.
Many rivers, often small urban ones, carry ocean plastic, so action on land matters most.
Microplastics can be removed from rivers quite easily once they have formed in the water.
questions.e: The passage traces ocean plastic to rivers, reports that the load is spread across many small urban streams and concludes that the street is the best place to act. The 'few giant rivers' view is the earlier estimate that later work revised.

questions.s: According to the passage, a great river may release less plastic than a small urban one because
o: large rivers flow too slowly to carry any plastic at all
large rivers are cleaned more often before the monsoon
small rivers hold more fish that swallow the plastic
much of a large river's waste is trapped on banks and in reservoirs
questions.e: The second paragraph says a great river's waste is trapped along hundreds of kilometres of banks and reservoirs. Cleaning before the monsoon is mentioned for urban channels, not for large rivers.

questions.s: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the later view described in the second paragraph?
o: Short city streams near the coast carried far more plastic than long inland rivers.
One large Asian river was found to carry more water than any other river in its region.
Turtles in the open ocean were more often tangled in fishing nets than in plastic bags.
Fragments of plastic were found in drinking water far away from any river at all.
questions.e: The later view holds that many short urban streams near the sea release large amounts of plastic, so finding them far more loaded than long inland rivers supports it. The volume of water a river carries says nothing about how much plastic it delivers.

questions.s: The final sentence suggests that the cheapest way to reduce river plastic is to
o: build larger floating barriers out in the open ocean
collect and manage waste before it reaches drains and rivers
dredge river beds in order to remove the microplastics
stop using rivers as a source of drinking water
questions.e: Naming the street as the cheapest place means dealing with waste before it enters drains and rivers, before it breaks into fragments that cannot be collected. The passage says microplastics are effectively impossible to remove, so dredging for them contradicts it.

questions.s: Which choice best summarises the passage?
o: A young doctor makes a serious error on her first night and is then reported by a nurse.
On her first night shift, a new doctor is quietly helped by a veteran nurse.
A nurse teaches a young doctor how to knit during a long and quiet night at the hospital.
A farmer's son helps a young doctor treat his father while the only nurse is busy elsewhere.
questions.e: Mahnoor falters, Shakeela supports her without fuss, the patient improves and Mahnoor reflects on what the night taught her. Losing the stethoscope for a second is not a serious error, and Shakeela praises good doctors rather than reporting anyone.

questions.s: When Mahnoor could not find her stethoscope, Shakeela
o: handed it to her from the desk without a word
told the patient's son to wait outside the room
went to fetch a new one from another ward
told her where it was in front of the patient
questions.e: The third paragraph says that without a word Shakeela handed her the stethoscope, which had been lying on the desk. Telling her aloud in front of the patient is the opposite of the silent help described.

questions.s: Shakeela's habit of asking "Doctor, shall I also...?" suggests that she
o: is unsure of her own duties and needs to be told what to do
wants the patient's son to see that she is really in charge
disagrees with most of the instructions Mahnoor gives her
guides Mahnoor tactfully while leaving her in charge
questions.e: By naming the step Mahnoor was about to forget as a polite question, Shakeela fills the gap while letting the doctor give the orders. Her thirty years of experience and calm action rule out the idea that she is unsure of her duties.

questions.s: Shakeela's remark that "the good doctors are the ones who listen on the second night too" implies that
o: most new doctors leave the district hospital after a single night
doctors who listen to their patients never need help from nurses
good doctors keep accepting help even after their first fear has passed
the second night on call is usually much harder than the first one
questions.e: On a first night, fear makes any doctor accept help; the remark praises those who keep listening once they feel confident. Nothing in the passage says the second night is harder; the point is about attitude, not difficulty.
